From over the wild Atlantic And wash of the Western seas, A voice came like the murmur Of summer among the trees. As sweet as the innocent laughter From children at their plaY, Yet fraught with the deepest wisdom Of men ef an older day. And never an English household But felt its tender thrill Like the weird Xolian music Of a harp on the window-sill. It came to man and maiden Like the swelling of midnight ch:naes, And they knew that the heart of the singer Was beating in the rhymes.

He came to the careworn toiler As be stood 'mid the smoky throng, And his tears would start in rapture At the marvellous gift of song. For it told the beautiful story That memory still keeps green As the murmuring pines and the hemlocks Toe tale of Evangeline. It told of Hiawatha, And of Laughing Water's graces In the lay that for future ages Embalms a vanished race. And the dower of German legend Was cullel by the master's skill, And offered a fragrant posy 'that all may keep who will. The New World and the Old World Joined hinds in each liquid line, Where the myrtle of classic culture Was wreathed with the Western pine. And never a word he uttered But straight to the heart it dew, As soft as the summer gloaming, As pare as the morning dew. 0 dear dead voice of the singer Whose magical notes are o'er, Our hearts are true to tha mmdc That echoes for evermore. 0 poet, thy runes are symbolled By the grave plot's sacred dowers; 0 death, where is thy conquest? His immortal songs are oars.

"A great loss to us, sir," repliel the waiter, shaking his head, "he had all his ale rent in from this 'armee i" PRINCESS L.LICE'S RESTORS.TION TO FAITR.-She had just returned irons her iesdian trip, into which she had thrown herself with true enjoyment and was still resting after the fatigue of the long journey. The,two little Princes had been playing by her sofa; Prince Ernest ran into the neat room follewed by the Princess, and in her brief absence, Prince Fritz fell out of the window upon the stone pavement below. One moment in the most vivid radiant life and health-, the next he lay senseless and craehed. He died a few boars later in his mother's arms. In her agony she sounded as it were for the first time, the depths of scepticism. She searched in vain through the various eveterns of philosophy, but found no foothold. 'She did not speak of the transformation that was going on within; but slowly, silently, and 'merely faith returned to her, never , again to falter. "The whole edifice of philosophical con- clusions which I had built up for myself, I find to have no 'foundation whatever—nothing of it is left—it has crumbled away like dust. What should we be, what would become of as, if we had no faith—if we did not believe that there is anOcid who rules the world and each single one of us?" ---Miss Gladstone in Contemporary Review._ Deena' "DON'T" TCO MUCH.—Life for some people is one perpetual "don't." Our sympathies were recently en- listed for Freddie, a little fellow of five, who had been kept within doors during a long storm. His mother,'a gentle woman, set quietly sewing, as she chatted with a friend. "'Don't do that, Freddie," she said, as the child's whip- 'bandit b-at a light tattoo on the carpet. A stool fell with a crash. "Don't make a noise, Freddie." The boy turned ,to the window, thenrcetless fingers makirg vague pictures on the damp pane. "Don't mark the window, Freddie," interposed the mother; and "Don't go into the hell." she added, as ha opened the door to escape. The " Don'ts " •continuel at brief intervals. At leng.h the small one, -seating hitnself With a *pathetically redgeed air, remained perfectly still for Itbout a minute. Then, with a long- drawn sigh. he asked, "Mamma, is there anything I can do?" There is no surer way to check confidential inter- course bet Ween parent and child, and to retard the develop- .ment of his best faculties, than to creete an atmosphere of blame about him. Ee will grow unhappy and discouraged, if notdisobedieat and reckless. Far better let some childish wrong-doings pass unreproved than to make your boy feel that km never quite pleases you. Wise commendation will not fester vanity or self-commionsness. I lovicg word, an appreciative, smile, any sympathetic recognition of real effort, is generally more helpful than many reproofa for 1 'failures. Check evil propensities by developing good ones, I 'rather than by waging a fierce, direct war of extermination. I I The result of such training may not be soon apperent, but din the end your child's character will be broader and Intronger. Wait for the moral nature to grow; and be I patient, as God is patient with His children. 1 1 Tun OLD TESTAYENT IN RELIGION.—A distinguished 1 I scholar, whose name 'is well known throughouteEurope as ' almost the symbol for ecientific inquiries on this field, said 1 but two months ago to me, "If you want to prove the I truth, the wisdom, the sober and honest history- of the i Bible, and the parity of ite religion, place it among the 1 Sacred Books of the Earl. In these books there are many i grains of gold, but they are hid in mountains of the most I extraorniaary rubbish; and the extraordinary thing is that ' it is the rubbish that calls forth the enthusiasm and admi. I ration cf the peoples that own them. The sobriety of the ' Bible, the purity of itsepirit, the elevation and devotion of its tone, make it occupy an entirely unique place. Placed among the Sacred Books of the East the contract would I I make its truth only the more stand out." Simply as a piece of literature it is the most marvellous thing in the world. You call it a Book, but it tands there a literature, the creation-cf from twelve to fifteen hundred years, in fragments, some small, others larger., each frag- ment ref-ecting its own age, the earliest being most dis- similar and strange to the latest; yet with all its distance, and all its variety, this Borne stands so near to us that it is to our spirits of all books the nearest in the world. 4t con- tains, ''ram the literary point of view, the most remarkable code of anoient times. It contains the quaintest, most beautiful, and graphic history. It oontains the supreme devotional literature of the world, the literature that men in their highest moments of religious transport or of pious meditation have used in en-press thoughts too deep for tears. It contains poetry that, simply as poetry, stands foremost in its own order, fall of a great sense of mystery, fall of an awful sense of suffering, pierced and transformed by a glorious sense of God. It possesses more than all a conception cf God and an idea e man, without aeparallel in the literature and religions of the ancient world. That Book ;s the noblest heirloom of humanity. To every man it belongs as an inalienable birth- right. To its best traths, to ite inmost heart, to its mean- inn, for this and all times, you have cc l eal an ihe Lzfe , indefe7 Tlble. right. —From " Religion in History at day." By A. 3f. Fairtairn, D.D. PROGRESS DUE TO INDIVIDUALS, NOT GOVERNMENTS.— Such an interpretation soon brings us to the inference that of the aggregate results of men's desires seeking their grati- fications, those which have prompted their private activities and their spontaneous co-operations have done much more towards soo:al development than those which have worked through governmental agencies. 'That abundant crops Row grow where once only wild berries could be gathered is due to the pursuit of individual satisfactions through many Centuries. The progress from wigwams to good houses has resulted from wish ee to increase personal welfare; and towns have arisen under the like promptings. Beginning with traffic at gatherings on occasions of religious festivals, the trading organisation, now so extensive and complex, has been produced entirely by men's efforts to achieve their private ends. Perpetually Governments have thwarted and deranged the growth, but have in no way furthered it, save by partially discharging their proper function and main- taining social order. So, too, with those advances of know- ledge and those improvements of appliances by which these structural changes and these increasing activities have been made possible. It is not in the State that we owe the mul- titudinous useful inventions from the plough to the tele- phone; it is not to the State which made possible extended navigation by a developed astronomy; it is not the State which made the discoveries in physics, chemistry, and the red, which guide modern manufacturers; it is not the State which devised the machinery for producing fabrics of every kind, for transferring men and things from place to place, and fcr ministering in a thousand ways to our com- forts. The world-wide transactions conducted in merchants' officee, the rush of traffic filling our streets, the retail dis- tributing system which brings everything within easy reach and delivers the necessaries of life daily at our doors, are lim rroteaarycyof mti no: ae theseon ae roonff mental origin. Hume, Kelso.- WHAT /9 THE LESSON OF THE CONFERENCE ?—This was the question put by Dr. Bond, of Gloucester, at the close of the recent very successful dairy week, which was due to his able initiation and organisation. "It is not far to seek," he said, in reply. "It is the necessity of providing sys- tematic instruction for thooe who engage in dairy work." The practice hitherto has very generally been to learn to makteGloucester cheese, Cheddar, or Stilton cheese pretty much as you learn to milk. You teach yourself—or such help as you receive is from some one who has himself or herself learnt—just by practice. He or she, too, never was "taught." The instruction, such as it leas, had been a mere family tradition. No other art or profession has been so entirely without a scientific or even systematic training. BUTTERINE PROHIEITED IN NEW YORK STATE.—The 'Cleo-margarine Bill has passed the Yew York State Legisla- ture, and received the consent of Governor Cleveland. The preamble of the bill states that it is "to prevent deception in sales of dairy products." It is every strict measure, and the most important clause of it is No. 6, which is as fol- lows:—" That no person shall manufacture out of any oleaginous substance or substances, or any compound of the same other than that produced from unadulterated milk or of cream from the same, any article designed to take the place of butter or cheese produced from pure, unadultered milk or cream of the rime; or shall sell or offer for sale the same as an article ti 2 food. Thic provision shall not apply to pure skimonilk cheese made from pure skins milk. Who- ever violates the provisions of this section shall be guilty of a mUdemeanocr, and shall be punished by a fine of not less than 100 dolts, nor more than 500 dole , or not lessthan six months' nor more than one year's imprisonment for the first offence, and by imprisonment for one year for etch subse- geent offeece." So far as New York State is concerned, this puts an end to the butterine trade within ite confines It is only erquestion of time now when the manufacture and sale of butterine will be prohibited through the whole of the Union. PLO/WRING IN GREEN CROPS AS A MANURE.—Now that the time has come round for adopting this old-faehioned coarse of husbandry I urge it strongly. Many old and prac- tical fencers tell me that it is a first-rate plan, and have seen wonderful results. Mustard is generally used, although more expensive as to seed. Vetches are better, having a larger growth and more foliage.,-hence absorbing more car- bon. Strange as it seems, many have asserted that they would rather plough in green crops than have them eaten by corn-fed sheep, the after effect on the land being more permanent and endurable. The beat time to plough in is just when the foliage is in bloom, not after, as then the seed begins to mature. I have spent some years in the United States, where the cropping is most exhaustive, crop following crop tilt the land is completely worn out, no manure being apoliml. It is then rested, and for .several ye ire recuperated by a succession of green crops or clever plumbed in. In the case of ploughing in lattermath clover or vetches it is better to have it mown directly in front of the plough, then cause it to be pushed in, in the farrow, that burying it bompletely ; a wheel pressure following is better still, as the compression causes the vegetable matter to rot quicker, and a crop of mustard or buckwheat can be sown directly on the top of that, to be ready to plough up for wheat or any grain crop, and so get two crepe to plough in instead of one. Mustard or buckwheat should not be sown later than the end of July. Another advantage is that it saves much labour and expense in cleaning fordfallows, as it completely stifles couch and weeds.—" Agricola," in Mark Lane Express. ENSILAGE.—CurrERs AND ELEVATORS.—In connection with the Bath and West of England Show last week ex- tensive experiments in the cutting and storage of silage were carrb d out by Mr. H. A. Brassey, M.P., of Preston Hall, Maidstone. Rye, on a field of about fifty acres, close to the show, had been grown. This was cat by several sheaf-binding reaping machines' and was at once carted to some half-a-dozen silos which had been erected at oncend of the field. It was then cut into 1-inch chaff by two machines manufactured for the purpose by Messrs. Bast, of Winterton, and Mrs. R. A. Lister and Co., of Dareley. The cut silage had to be delivered into the silos from the cutters, and to ensure this Messrs. Bust employed a powerful blow- ing fan, which was attached to their machine. This, how- ever, did not work well, as the chaffed fodder was not pro- perly conveyed to the silo, and flew about in all directions. Messrs. Lister and Co. carried their cut material on a nar- row elevator, fitted with an endless band, which enabled them to deliver the fodder to either of the silos without difficulty. A weighing machine was fixed in the ground over which the laden carts had to pass, so that the quantity out by each machine was accurately ascertained, Messrs. Lister and Co.'s machine, which cut vn an average upwards of two hundredweight per minute, or six tone an hour, was purchased by Mr. Brassey. The tilos were fitted with different modes of compreesing the fodder, and the systems of Messrs. Reynolds and Co., Mr. Champion, and others, as stated in our report of the show last week, were practically demonstrated. These experiments were conducted on each day of the show, excepting Thursday, which was observed as a holiday by Mr. Brassey's workpeople. DAIRY HOMESTEADS.—AS many readers are interested in dairy homesteads and farms, it will be well to notify that most valuable prizes have been this year offered by the British Dairy Farmers' Association for designs for dairy homesteads. The buildings are to be designed so as to be suitable for a tenant farmer's requirements on a farm of 180 acres, of which 165 are meadow and pasture and 15 arable, the rent being £3,600. A sum el £720 may be spent on the erection of the dwelling-hones, but the total cost of the buildings, drains, and fence walls, including the house, Is not to exceed £2.520. Provision must be allowed for the winter hou,ing of no less a qaantity of stock than the fol- lowing :—Thirty-four cows in milk, 14 cows barren or dried off for calving, 12 in-calf stirks, heifers two years old; 12 yearlings, 20 rearing calves, one bull, three horses, one year- ling horse, one foal, one breeding sty for pigs, and two sties fcir store pigs. Besides a shed for carts and implements and the necessary accommodation for storing and preparing food, the design must provide for the building of a silo capable of holding 80 tons of ensilage, and also a poultry-house having a floor space of 75 superficial feet. If covered yards are adopted, each cow is to receive at least 100 superficial feet of floor space each mirk 85 feet, and each yearling 50 feet. The dwelling-house is to have the following accommoda- tion :—A cellar in the basement; on the ground plan—par- boar, front kitchen, a scullery or back kitchen (having a floor space of at least 200 superficial feet) and a pantry. It is left to the judgment of competitors as to what the size and position of the dairy buildings shall be. The usual offices are to be shown, while there most be means for erect- ing not less than form good bedrooms, each with an open fireplace, on the first floor. CRUELTY TO ANIMALS FROM A VETERINARY POINT OF View.—The committee appointed by the British National Veterinary Congress of 1881 to consider the subject of cruelty to animals from a veterinary point of view, on the basis of a paper read at the congress by Mr. W. Hunting, F.R.C.V.S., of London, has just issued its report. The com- mittee agrees in the main with Mr. Hunting's views as ex- pressed in his very able Paper, and has made the following public declaration in the name of the profession represented by the congress, and each subject has been treated briefly, in order, to quote the words of the committee, that "a code may be found to guide the public on the points respectively raised" :—Lameness may be painters or painful. Those cases where the lameness passes off with 'exercise are,prima facie, cases being accompanied by pain. This specially ' applies to cases of navicular disease and spavin. In such 'casts horses ought not to be worked, and when worked it is cruelty. Gingering is decided cruelty. Wounds are not t causes of unfitness for work, unless pressed upon by harness or effected by the movements of the animal. Twitching: The practice called "twitching" causes acute pain, and is frequently unjustifiable, especially when a twitch is used by stablemen and others in charge of horses. Burning Gums for " Lampas" is cruelty. Knocking out Wolf Teeth is cruelty. Extracting Temporary Teeth, save for surgical -reasons, is cruelty. Caeration of male animals is necessary, but should be performed in the least painful manner and by a skilled operator. Spaying of female ani- mate is unnecessary, and ought to be abolished. Parturi- tion: Unnecessary pain is often inflicted by ignorant per- Reno when attempting to deliver the young by forcible and cruel means.. A skilled and experienced veterinary surgeon should always be called in to render assistance in difficult cases. Operations of various kinds arc frequently performed on animals by ignorant persons, and much cruelty is caused thereby, which ought to he publicly deprecated and pre- vented by law. All painfcl operatione not required for the good of the animal operated on are of a cruel nature. No' operations causing pain to an animal should be performed by an unskilful puma. All necessary operations ought to be performed in a scientific manner, and by the most humane] methods, in order thereby to prevent the infliction of-nn-1 necessary Fait. , PROFESSOR SHELDON ON DAKRYlNG.—Proressor Sheldonl has this week delivered a lecture on the English dairy, at' the International Ifealth Exhibition. He showed that. dairy farming has suffered, in common with the growing of corn and the raising of sheep, by the recent wet seasons. Neither plants nor animals can flourish when the ground has become water-sodden, and the considerable reduction which has taken place in the number of cattle in the British Islands since 1874—though the deficiency is now being rapidly overtaken—puts into tangible form the heavy losses which have been sustained. Ten years gime the total num- ber of cattle in these islands was 10,281,036 ; in 1878 the number sank to 9,761,288 • last year it reached 10,097,943; and it is regarded as probable that the figures for the cur- rent year will again mount up to those of a decade ago Fine weather is essential to healthy stook, and midsummer now finds farmers almost complaining of the excessive fine- ness. It may snit cattle, but what of the bay crop ? Professor Sheldon estimates the tenants' capital in vol,,ed in dairy farming at nearly £200,000,000, and the landlord,' capital at £1,400,000,000; the total thus equalling !mica ,

the amount of the national debt. It is almost too late in the day to expect that anything new can be said respecting the dietetic value of milk, still few persons are aware how nearly it approximates to flesh diet. The professor says three pints of milk are equal to lib. of beef, so that at that rate milk at 4d. per quart would be the exact equivalent of beef at 61(1. per lb.; or if the meat were taken at 71-d. per lb., the milk ought to fetch 53. per quart. Notwithstanding its unequalled nutritive qualities, the average quantity of mils consumed in these islands is approximately given at

„ only a little over three pints per head per week ; butter reaches 3,10z5. per head per week, and cheese about 4ozs. London consumes something like £26,000 worth of milk per day, viz., about 1,250,000 quarts, reckoned at 6d. per quirt; ot batter the value consumed amounts to £45,000 tor day, or £16,000,000 per annum. Speaking of substi- tutes for butter, and cattle disease, as the two principal things against which dairy farmers have to contend, the lecturer said they had no right to complain against bat-

terine so long as it was honestly told as Ellleil, and that intelligent farmers did net object to the introduction of foreign meat, but only to the importation of disease. On the whole, the future of the British dairy farmer is cer- tainly promising. He produces three of the most essential as well as every-day articles of mnsamption. He will have difficulty to keep pace with the increase of his customers, provided he maintains the quality of his products ; but should he neglect this all-important condition, foreign competition will speedily and effectually crowd him out of the market in respect to at least two of them—butter and cheese. BIRKENHEAD AGRiCIILTIMAL Snow.—The 42nd annual show of the Wirral and Birkenhead Agricultural Society was commenced on Wednesday at the permanent showground at 13idston, near Birkenhead. and was continued till last evening. Among the numero 18 attractions in the she wy ard, in addi- tion to the magnificent display from a purely agricultural point of view, which included stock, implements of hus- bandry, dp., one of the most prominent was the presence of the famous band of the Coldstream Guards, which executed a lengthy programme each day of the show. The society's dietricris this year extended, so as to include all parts both of Cheshire and Lancashire within twenty. five miles of the Birkenhead Town Hall, instead of being, as heretofore, con- fined to the Hundred of Wirral; and the farmers residing in the enlarged district have responded very well indeed to the opportunity afforded them of entering their stock for com- petition on the same terms as other members of the society. The result is that the entries are more numerous in nearly all the classes this year than last, the total increase being over 160 entries. This 'year's figures are as follow :—Horses 266, cattle 109, sheep 69, pigs 31, poultry 241, pigeons 205. dogs-410, and butter 49. The prize money amounts to nearly £l,OOO, besides various medals, there being awarded in the Implement department alone no fewer than five gold medals and' 15 silver medals. The show of horses, as may be in- ferred front the large number of entries, was the finest ever seen in the yard, and the farmers and gentlemen of the dis- trict are to be congrattilated on the possession of such a magnificent display of horseflesh. So evenly balanced were the merits of the animals in several of the classes, that the judges were induced to award commended tickets to all the entries after the prize winners. Cattle were very good all over, but of high merit in the open classes, which included a number of animals intended to be shown at the forthcom- ing Royal Show. Young bulls, dairy cows, and heifers were a large and creditable show. The entries in sheep were more numerous than at any previous show, and included the stock Of many noted breeders. THE ROYAL COMMISSIONERS' REPORT ON AGRICULTURAL EDUCATION. NO. IV. Leaving Germany', and dealing with France, the Royal Commissioner observes that the French system of agricul- tural education is in principle the antithesis of the German; that is to say it is based on a combination of practice with science. It differs in its higher stages from the German in another very important respect—namely, that attendance at lectures and in the laboratories is as compulsory as in the lower schools. Failure to pass a satisfactory examination at the end of each term or year, as the case may be, at once severs the pupil from his connection with the school without any action being taken by anybody, and the pupil cannot be reinstated without a special order from the Minister of Agriculture. The connection of the pupils with even the highest agricultural schools in France is thus eminently real and practical, whereas at the German Uni- versity it is too often illusory or merely theoretical. An , entrance examination is generally exacted unless in the case of the higher schools the candidate has already obtained the degree of Bachelor of Sciences. The right to the one year's voluntary service in the army without further ex- amination is attached to the entrance certificate of the , higher schools, and to the final certificate of the lower schools—namely, "Practical schools of agriculture," and "Farm schools." The importance of this privilege to pupils of the lower schools is very great, because instead of spending five years in the army it enables them to devote two or three years to acquiring technical instruction in their I future business, either without payment or by paying a por- tion of the cost of their board and lodging. Compulsory military service is an element which requires to be con- stantly borne in mind when it is attempted to estimate the adaptability of the French or German systems of agricul- tural education to our circumstances, and it is not a little . remarkable that it does not operate more powerfully to at- tract pupils to the farm schools in France. The first agri- • cultural school in France appears to have been founded at . La Eochette, near Melon, in 1763, and in 1771 a second was I established at Annel, near Compiegne. In 1822 Mathieu de Dombaste took the farm of Roville, measuring 250 acres, on . a lease of 20 years, and a number of his admirers placed a . sum of £l,BOO at his disposal to enable him to found a • school of agriculture. Here he demonstrated that the old three-field system might be profitably replaced by alternate t cropping, and his pupils, carrying his principles throughout t the length and breadth of France, created a rural revolu- tion. This school disappeared at the death of its founder, but in 1827 Auguste Bella founded the celebrated e4tBhen the Practical cAtabliehed three . school of agriculture at Grignon. In 1830 M. Rieffel founded a farm school at Grand-Jonan, and in 1841 1 this became the Regional School of the west of France.grades f The law agriculturalo f schools. s 3rdi,nclt3 schools of agriculture, the Departmental professors, and the , Agronomic stations have all been created, so that at present the means of instruction in agriculture in France and Algeria are represented by one National Institute, three regional schools, nine practical schools, two shepherds' schools, 23 farm schools, one school of horticulture at Versailles, four email schools of horticulture, 23 agronomic stations, and 55 departmental professors of agriculture. The Institut Agronomiquo is the highest school of agriculture in France, and stands on about the same level as the Berlin High School. Thia institute was splendidly established in one of the buildings belonging to the Palace of Versailles. Attached to it were three large farms, furnished with collec- tions of numerous breeds of horses, cattle, sheep, and pigs. The professors were all eminent men, and did much good to the country. In 1852, by a decree of the Prind-President, the institute was closed, but in 1876 it was restored by an Act passed by M. Eug. Tiaserand, the Inspector General of agriculture. Nearly one half of the pupils at this institute are the eons of landowners intending to farm their own pro- perties, and the other half is composed of Government 411cers in the department of agricultural professors, direc- tors of agricultural experimental stations, d irectors of sugar Manufactories, &c., agricultural engineers, large tenant
\ I

farmers or managers for agricultural companies in Algeria, I dzo. The complete course of study to enable a student to obtain the diploma extends over two years, but some students having obtained their diploma, especially those who wish to become agricultural chemists, may remain a third year, during which they work chiefly in the chemical laboratory, and at the experimental farm. The students are bound to em.

ploy a portion of their vacations in studying practicall agriculture on farms, and that they must bring back with them a report on the farms visited, and on all the opera- tions which have taken place during their stay. The course of study is most thorough, and the practical exercises com- plete. Mr. Rister thinks that the two years' course of study is too short, and suggests a three years' course, and it is probable that, wi•h some few modifications, his views will be adopted. Students pay only £l2 per annum for in- , struction, but at the commencement of each year they mot deposit an additional sum of 48s. with the secretary towards the cost of excursions, breakages stn. They find their own board, lodging, books, and other requirements. Every year there are in each division two students who receive a bursary of £4O a year, and two of £2O a year, together with free instruction, and there are eight others who have no fees to pay. In 1882 this school cost the State £10,058. There were 88 ordinary students, seven who were contina• lug their studies a third year, together with 26 free audi- tors. Thus the cost of the 95 students entails a cost to the State of about 100 guineas per head per annum, in addition to the fees which they pay. Every year the two students who stand at the head of the list receive traval in; scholar- ships available either for France or foreign countries, The most celebrated of the three regional schools of agri- culture is Grignon. The school was estab ished in 1827. The est ste, cons sting of 1,160 acres, was let to a company by the French Government bra period of 40 years, and the school was maintained by the company until 1838, when the State undertook the payment of the professors and other costs of instruction, besides endowing the institution with a certain number of bursaries. At the expiration of the lease a portion of the iand was let to a tenant, but 700 acres were retsined, being attached to the school establish- ment. The farm arrangements are superior in every respect. An entrance examination for adtaissi.n to the s3hool must be passed by all candid des who have not taken the d-gres of bachelor pf science. The chief subjects of study are agriculture, rural economy, zootechnics,agricultural engin • eering and tnechanics,hotany, sylviculture, physics, chemis- try, technology, arboriculture, market gardening, hygiene, and agricultural book-keeping. The total number of stu- dents is 100, making an entry of about 40 every year, con- sidering that the whole course extends over 21 years. Of the students in 1881, 18 were the EMS of proprietor farmers, six tenant farmers, and 14 of other professions. The stu- dents pay £4B per annum for instruction, board, lodging, fire, lighting, and washing. The cost of the school to the State in one year was £7,080. The young men learn at Grignon, both theoretically and practically, all the most perfect methods of cultivation. The ba-is of intermediate schools which have been estab- lished in France is a kind of co•operation between the State, the Depart nent, and the Director. These intermediate schools meet the wants of the sons of cultivators in somewhat easy circumstances—young men who require a more scientific education than could be given at the farm schools, bat who either could not afford to pay the comparatively high price of the original schools, or whose previous education was not sufficiently advanced to enable them to pass the entire examination. The State pays the salaries of the Difector of these schools and the teaching staff; the Department pays the expenses of the equipment of the school, and the Director undertakes to give an approved education at a moderate cost. Notwithstanding official encouragement, it is remarkable that only six parochial schools of agriculture had been established up to the end of 1881. The most per- fect of these schools is at Les Merchines, near Vanbumrt, in the department of ths Meuse. It consists of 750 acres of land in a ring fence; the farm buildings are new and ex- cellently designed, most of the domestic work was done by sisters belonging to a religious body, and order and neatness prevails everywhere. Dealing with lower agriculture edu- cation. the Commissioner says that on the farm schools of France, a certain number of young men' sons of labourers and small farmers, receive at these schools a fair amount of scientific and general instruction, and a good practical training in farm work, free of cost to the parents.—We shall complete the report on France next week.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

CELERY.—If advantage is taken immediately after rain to draw an inch of soil over the whole surface of the trench, it will save watering for a time by preventing evaporation. We would also resort to the same expedient after the plants have received a watering, so that the water will reach the lowest roots. It is of the utmost importance that the water applied to celery and other plants should be exposed to the atmosphere for several hours before it is used. The tem- perature of cold spring water at this season of the year will be about 50 deg., and that of the earth surrounding the roots 60 deg. The temperature of the soil is an important factor in deciding the quality and earliness of crops, and accounts for the lateness of crops on cold, ill-drained soil compared with that of a lighter nature. It is obvious that frequent waterings at the temperature given will have the effect of keeping the heat of the soil 10 deg. lower than it would be, whilst to make waterings as stimulating as pos- sible the temperature of the water should be a few degrees higher than the soil, which is not always practicable. The nearest to it is pond water, and river water comes next. The soap-suds on washing days should be always reserved for celery, for independent of its warmth it contains potash, an indispensable agent to build up plant structure. BROAD BRANS.—If a portion of those in flower have the tops pinched, they will form leaves earlier than if allowed to extend themselves. We always endeavour to stop all our broad beans. By doing this at intervals, we have suc- cessional crops. Paes.—Where the sticks for these are costly, pea nets will be found cheaper in every way. Peas requiring present supports may have a few rough sticks laid along the row, and to these the plants will cling. If the sticks are branched, they will prevent the haulm lying on the ground. A string stretched over the plants after their heads are turned in the direction of the sticks will help to keep them down.

LETTIME.-Our earliest are now fit for tying, though many have formed good white hearts without this assist- ance. Tying makes the cos lettuce ready for use quite ten days earlier, and their fitness for use may be prolonged by supplying them with plenty of water in dry weather. Tying must not be performed when there is moisture on the leaves, nor when they are warm from the heat of the sun; neither must the ligatures be drawn too tight. In- attention to these matters will cause the centre to decom- pose.

Tux Fuosx GARDEN.—WHITE PINKS.—What a glaring anomaly the cynic will say. But it is nothing of the sort. Pink is the family name, and many of the members are of that hue, but the subject under notice is of dissimilar com- plexion. The White Pink is the sweetest herbaceous flower that adorns the front garden at this season of the year. Its spicy odour is agreeable to most people. The purity of its colour and the elegant fimbriated petals demand for it a con- spicuous place in the bridal bouquet, or on the breast of the most fastidious " button-hole " connoisseur. Why such a chaste floral gem should not find a place in every front gar- den is beyond our comprehension. Those who may be for- tunate to possess it will find that twiggy branches of the requisite length will be the beat supports for the flowers, which become too heavy for their stalks in rainy weather. If the bottom end is pointed they may be inserted amongst the flowers as required, and the latter will rest in the forked spaces.

THE WINDOW.—Callas, or Arum Lillies, should be planted out if strong plants are required. They do not increase in height by this treatment, but the dimensions of the stem are greatly augmented. They also give considerably less trouble than when kept in pots. The soil they are planted in may be one•fourth manure, and much of the soil surrounding the roots may be shook off. In planting the fresh soil should be nearly two inches deep over the roots, and that surround- ing them should be made moderately firm. A stake should be placed to each plant, and a string tied round it, or it will slip down. Next draw the string round the leaves, and tie the ends so as to form a band that will support them in all weather.

His life is an enigma, a forlorn and never-ending search after the true, the beautiful, and the good.—Alger. THE SUTTON Tironrc.—The Stonyhurst Magazine, in ad. dition to a large amount of antiquarian matter relating to the College, contains the narrative of one who went to view the alleged mid-winter flowering of the Sutton thorn. This forms curious reading, and may be quoted:—" We went to see the tree last Twelfth-night eve. We certainly very plainly saw it in a very forward state, viz., in leaf, with a large portion in full bud, surrounded by a large crowd of eager spectators, who pressed about it, and made anything like steady observation extremely difficult. Some lamps were hung around and in the tree itself, but the wind prevented a very clear inspection. At about twelve, mid- , night, some cried out,' I see some flowers now.' Others as twelve struck, cried, There are some more out.' drc. I kept my eyes fixed on a spray covered with unopened buds near me, and I believe that they came flower at the very stroke of twelve, but I confess thelight was not good pnough for me to be absolutely certain if the others were correct in their lemarks. H., who is of a sceptical dispositi in, and who was strongly opposed to the idea of anything marvellous about it, declared that the branch he watched did nothing at all, and there is no doubt that when, at 12 15, we left the orchard, at least three-fourths nf the buds were still unopened. Then the crowd grew impatietft and riotobs, and climbed up in defiance of all older and regulation, !Ail- ing off the branches, and finally leaving it stripped bare. So the problem remains still unsolved. I questioned many others. All saw bads burst at twelve p.m. Some declare that in other years the tree only began to bloom at twelve p.m., and did not fully do so until one am. My own belief is that the poor tree was doing its best to do its duty, but was not allowed fair play."

Flinn, Main, and Montgomery. —Oracle. A NEVE SHIPBUILDING MATERIAL.—It is well known that vessels built of thin steel will rust through rapidly if not kept conetantly painted. This is found to .be the case to a remarkable extent in such vessels when navigating the rivers draining the interior of the African continent, the waters of which possess the power of corroding and eating through steel plates very rapidly. It. has occurred to Mr. A. Dick, of 110, Cannon-street, London, the inventor of the new alloy known as "delta metal," to apply it to ship- building purposes, as it successfully resists corrosive action.' A steam launch called the Delta has therefore been built en- tirely of this metal, and is at the Crystal Palace Inter- national Exhibition. The length of the launch over all is 36f t., with a breadth of beam of sft. 6in., and a depth from gunwale to keel of 3ft., the vessel being capable of seating conveniently 25 persona. Delta metal, which is an alloy of copper, zinc, and iron, having been proved by repeated ex- periments to be equal in strength, ductility, and toughness to mild steel, the plates and angle pieces are of the same thickness they would be if steel were used—viz, 3-32 of an inch. The engine is of the usual direct-acting inverted type, and of sufficient•power to -give a epeed of from eight to nine miles an hour—Times, BACTERIA IN Buteks.---Referring to the alleged discovery by M. Parize of bacteria not only on the surface but in the interior of bricks, the Lancet calls the attention of the pub- lic to the fact that bacteria are not necessaril all hurtful. "We are not told," says the Lancet," precisely what sort of microorganisms were discovered, but it must be remem- bered that even bacteria are susceptible of classification into useful, harmless, and noxious. There is no good reason for being alarmed at the presence of these germs in burnt clay, for the atmosphere itself is known at times, probably always, to contain varying numbers of them. It is certainly not wise to connjure up new sanitary dangers on the receipt of information not alto- gether of a novel character. Let the public, therefore, not be alarmed.". We may add that what may be spoken of as the legitimate function of bacteria is still an open question. It is, for instance, a question how far they are useful in aiding the processes of digestion, and Dr. Angus Smith has even asked whether water entirely deprived of living organisms can be considered good or wholesome water in relation to the animal economy. The presence of living germs in burnt bricks is, however, apparently another curi- ous illustration of the varied conditions under which bacte- ria can live; and even if harmless bacteria are to be found in bricks it is not unlikely that deadly ones might be found there also. Meanwhile the alleged discovery may well at- tract the notice of M. Bechamp, who will probably be dis- posed to contend that the brick bacteria have been developed by the heating process from the geological microzymes in the original materials.

div.head: MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
div.p: THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
BRAHMAS.

A few years ago, of all the breeds of domestic poultry, perhaps that which was the greatest favourite was the Brahma. We do not mean so much amongst farmers as amongst small poultry keepers, though the former class, or at least such of them as tried to improve their stocks of fowls, generally resorted to Brahma cocks for this purpose, and we can yet see in the slightly-feathered legs to be found in many farmyards traces of this crossing. And there was at that time sufficient to warrant a use of Brah- mas, for they had one or two characteristics which are valuable and are sought after by farmers. First, they pos- sessed size, always a necessary thing where table birds are concerned, and weight is a great desideratum where the re- turn depends so much upon the size of the produce. Chickens, as a rule are small, and to many who produce fo eels for their own tables, any breed that will carry sufficient meat to allow cutting for a few persons naturally is in greater favour with them than those where, however tine the quality of meat, are only sufficient for a couple of per- sons, even with ordinary appetites. Thus, as the Brahma met such a requirement as this, they were and are still re- garded with more than ordinary favour by many poultry keepers, especially as, though they are not the finest flavoured of all fowls in flesh, they are, as young birds, by no means to be despised. Second, they are capital winter layers. Tile profuse feathering appears to keep the body warmer than with more scantily furnished fowls, and thus they, like most Asiatic birds, are good layers during the colder months of the year. It is true that the eggs are somewhat small, but they have the buff tint which is a favourite with many persons, and are, withal, rich in flavour. So that where winter eggs and size of bodies are regarded as attractive features, the Brahma has had, and has, many friends.

It is generally acknowledged that the Brahma was ori- ginally a cross-bred or manufactured breed, and probably more lies have been told respecting it than any other fowl. For many years there hung about its origin a mist of falsity and cross-swearing which was embarrassing to the ordinary poultry keeper, and many gallons of ink have been wasted over a controversy which, save in one or two re- spects, could do no good to any one. Various men claimed to be the originators of the varieties, for there are two of these, the lights and the darks, whilst others declared that they had introduced them from India or China or some- where else. Of course, the object of all this wa, to show that the individuals concerned not only deserved the honour and glory of their discovery or invention, but had in their yards the real stock, the only "Simon Pure," and that no- where else could the proper thing be obtained. This was sufficient to account for the whole thing. But testimony has shown that in India there exist fowls similar in all respects to the original birds, those shown twenty-five to thirty years ago, where they are known as Chittagongs, the name under which they were first known both in America and England. This refers to the light variety, and when dark birds were first bred, as they probably were obtained either from a sport or by crossing, these were called " Bar- ramnooters," afterwards to be altered to "Brahma Pootra," the latter half of which is generally dropped now, and hence we know them commonly as Brahmas, though there are old- fashioned people and schedulers that still retain the fuller title. Another term used was that of Shanghaes, and those who adopted it stated that the birds they owned came from the Chinese port of Shangbae ; but all these things have died down, the Brahma has taken its position, and ter years ago the controversy came to an end by sheer exhaustion, and we hope it may never be revived. Like most other new breeds the Brahma—for we will designate all the various kinds under that name—met with considerable opposition, but the present by an American fancier to, and the acceptance of a pair by, her Ilajesty the Queen, gave them a start. Like sheep follow- ing the bell-wether, so poultry keepers followed the Queen's example. What she put in her yard they must, and the breed soon became most popular, until a few years ago it stood first in the great Birmingham Poultry Show; and now, in nearly every show, it is first or pretty nearly so. But even the Queen's example would not have been suffcient to hold it in popular favour had it not possessed qualities of its own. In addition to those already named, it is a bird that can easily be made a pet of, is very tame, can be kept in by low fences, not being a flying fowl, and looks well on a rreen sward. It is hardy, also, standing confinement and unfavourable conditions very well. It must not be thought that it is a very heavy layer, for that it is not, and pro- bably ninety to one hundred eggs per annum is about the average of its produce But it is a good sitter and mother, ind its eggs come chiefly at a time when these are scarce, and they therefore give to the breed a better name than mere numbers would gain for it. The Brahma was a very different breed when first intro- duced to what we now can see. It was perhaps no smaller In actual size of body, but it had not such profuse plumage,

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—Mosnay. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at tour o'clock. Tan CONFERENCE —Lord GRANVILLE laid before the House the terms of the Anglo-French agreem-nt with res- Pact to the affairs of Ezypt. His lordship read copious ex- tracts from the despatches which had passed between him- self and M. Waddington, the French ambassador to the English Court, and from his lordship's statement of the result of these negotiations it appeared that the British oc- cupation might, at the discretion of the British Govern- Mont, be prolonged mail January let, 1888, and it was also Provided that the occupation might, if necessary, be further extended, unlese all the Powers agreed in taking exception in such a course. The French Government merle no pre- tensions to any revival of the Dual Control, ana undertook to send no troops into Egypt, unless with the concurrence of the British Government. In our own interests and that of Egypt it was extremely desirable that, without interfer- ing with politics or administration, the,- Caisse de la Date Publique " should be entrusted by the forthcoming Confer- ence with new powers, which would be of great practical use. —Lord SALISBURY did not think that the proposals as sub- mitted by the Foreign Secretary were reassuring They seemed to contain much that was perilous to the inter- ests of England, and to be full of men ace to the future Peace of the world. All the more difficult points were covered by studied ambiguity of language. There was the burning question of what was to be done supposing at the end of three years' time circumstances were not such as to Permit of the evacuation ef the country by the British troops, and there was the burning question of the jurisdic- tion and functions of the multiple control. The whole of the agreemeet evaded the main grounds on which the whole negotiations were undertaken, and did not touch the financial question which was the consideration which led England to approach the Foreign Powers at all—Lord JERSEY protested strongly against the agreement. It seemed to him that the Government had succeeded in tak- ing England into a Conference with one hand tied behind her back.—Both Lord Cairns and Lord Saliebury questioned Lord Granville with the view ef eliciting some information with regard to the financial arrangement, but his lordship would disclose nothing. He annensmed that the Confer- ence would meet on Saturday.—Their lordships shortly afterwards adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. THE CONFERENCE ON EGYPT. Mr. GLADSTONE, in announcing the negotiations with France in reference to the proposed Conference, said in the iaterval between iesuing the invitations and the meeting of the Conference France asked for preliminary explanatiens, and Her Majesty's Government merle a thorough investiga- tion into the condition of Egyptian finance with the view of preparing a plan to lay before the Conference. Her Majesty's Government were as ready to give the French Government explanations as the latter were to ask for them. The Prime Minister then proceeded to explain that there was a com- plete and final abondonment of the Dual Control, and that in the event of our leaving Egypt France should not enter the country except with our consent, so as to bring to an end the idea of the solitary action of any Power in Egypt. What we offered was offered was that until a definite term had arrived we bad reserved discretion to remain or not to remain, that the term should be January 1, 1888, and that after that term we should no longer remain in solitary occu- pation if the Powers of Europe declared that the state of the country was such as to permit of our departure without peril to its peace and order. There remained the modifica- tions required by the international arrangements to which Egypt was not subject There would be no general control over the Egyptian finances, and the budget would not be framed by the commissioners of the Khedive' so that every reasonable scope should be given to the development of that degree of independence which Egypt might fairly claim. There were three defined extensions of the powers of the Caisse, which the Government believed to be necessary alike for the welfare of Egypt, for the important financial interest of England that were now involved, and likewise for the interest of the creditors of Egypt. For this purpose the Caisse will receive a limited extension of 'its powers, and they aimed at two objects alone (1) to make sure that the Commission- ers of the Cahse shill be provided with sufficient informa- tion as to the financial procedure of the Government of Egypt, and haveipower to offer useful suggestions; and (2) that they shall have effective means of preventing excess in the Egyptian budget. The Caisse would be composed of four members, and the president of the commission was to be an Englishman. Mr. Gladstone went on to say that the two Governments of England and France had agreed that they should prepare a plan for the neutralisation of the Egyptian territory, and this plan would embrace the Suez Canal. This, however, was not a matter for immediate settlement; but everything he had spoked of was entirely contingent upon what was to be done in the Conference, and what was done in the Conference would again be contingent upon the approval of Parliament. The Government under- took to accelerate the decision of the Conference, and when that decision was arrived at net a day would be lost in sub- mitting it to Parliament. The plans they held would be favourable to the peace of Europe, to international law, and to civilisation and mankind, and if they did not meet the judgment of Parliament those who had framed them, and those who meant to adhere to them, ought not for one mo- ment longer to continue to be the Government of the country. (Cheers ) Sir S. NORTHCOTE thought there were grave objections to the plan, but he would not now enter into details. The period of our occupation raised a question of the most seri- ous character, requiring the judgment of the House as early as possible. He hoped some further information would be given as te the proposals to be put before the Conference. Lord R. CHURCHILL said he did not think anything more ludicrously shameful had ever been submitted by a Prime Minister to Parliament. He did not know whether to laueh at the folly of the Government or cry for the honour of his country. The gist of the statement was that France was to take the lead in Egypt. The assurances of the French Government were absolutely valueless, for who would dare to say that the Republic would be in existence to-morrow. Mr. Gseeesrenea explained that what he had said was not that France was to take the lead in Egypt, but that France was entitled to take the lead among the other Powers. Mr. GOSCHEN deprecated the idea'of the leader of the Opposition submitting a motion before the result of the Conference was known, for in that way Parliament would commit itself without knowing what action was to he taken by the other Powers. Mr. BOURKE protested against the policy of the Govern- ment in convoking a conference atoll, seeing that they had gone to Egypt in spite of the public law Of Europe. Sir. R. Caoss wanted to know whether the country would be called on in any way to provide motley for carrying out the arrangements of the Government. Mr. A. J. ItaLroun said the interest of the Egyptian people was being sacrificed in the name of international law. Mr. W. E. Foasran deprecated a premature expression of opinion on the part of the House. Lord JOHN Mi.NNERS contended that it was playing with the House not to submit the financial proposals before the Conference met. Mr. GLADSTONE, in replying, contended that it was impos- sible to submit the financial proposal to Parliament before the Conference met. When the oroper tines arrived Parlia- meat should be put in absolute possession of all the informa- tion the Government had. The debate then ended. THE FRANCHISE BILL. On the consideration of this bill as amended, Mr. ANDERSON proposed a clause providing that a con- *Chimney should have a claim on the services of Be member, and in the event of his absence for three months should have power to summon him to attend to his duties, and that on his failure for one month after that a new writ should be Issued.—The ATrORNEY-GENERAL opposed, and the clause was negatived. Mr. TOMLINSON then moved the following clause : " Every man who resided within a county or borough for a period of twelve months, but has not by reason of such resi- dence a qualification to be registered as a voter in such county or borough, may be registered as a voter, and may vote on proving that he has, in the year for which he claims to be so registered, paid or had deducted from the income of any real or personal property accruing to him during such year income or property tax to the amount of not less than 10s."—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL said that this ques- tion had already been discussed fully in committee. The chief objection to this clause was that it would lead to the creation of fagot votes.—The clause was rejected by 108 to 24. After this there was a long discussion on the disfranchise- ment of convicts.—Lord FOLKESTONE withdrew the clause which he had placed on the paper in favour of one moved by Mr. M. Lloyd, which disqualified for 12 months any per- son convicted and sentenced to penal servitude or imprison- ment with hard labour.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL accepted it with the addition that the conviction should be on indict- ment and by verdict of a jury, but this was warmly objected to by members below the gangway, and by the Irish Nationalist part'.—After a long and animated conversation, the second reading was carried by 114 to 81. Some time was afterwards spent in amending the details- In the first place, the words 'j an indictment" was carried by 198 to 31, and the words "by a Jury" were carried by 149 to 111.— Colonel Nowa; then moved the omission of the words "or any other crime," and in the course of the discussion on this, after the clause had occupied over three hours, Mr. GLADSTONE admitted that the Government had made a mis- take in agreeing to it, and would vote against the clause. The Government did believe that by the course they pur- sued they were meeting the decidedly prevailing feeling of the House. More than three hours had elapsed since this ill-starred amendment was introduced, and it was estimated that two or three days might be occupied in its turther dis- cussion. He would appeal to Colonel Nolan to withdraw his amendment, awl to Mr. Mogan Lloyd to withdraw the Clause, and he hoped the latter would agree with him that the game was not worth the candle. (Cheers and laughter.)—Colonel NOLAN .offered to withdrew his amend- Mont. and Mr. LLOYD expressed his willingness to withdraw the clause.—Leave to withdraw the amendment was at first refused, and the House was cleared for a division, but leave Was subsequently given.—An amendment moved by Sir ,11. thugs-BEAM, providing that a criminal plead- ing guilty shall be in the same position of dis- qualification, was inserted. On the question that the clause etand part of the bill, Mr. Remus acid Mr. GIBSON indul- ged in some caustic reflections on the levity and vacillation O the Government and the serious loss of time thus occa- ioned.--Mr. CLARKE and Lord FOLKESTONE spoke in the lale strain, and atter a motion to adjourn the debate had

been negatived by 174 to 89, the clause was rejected by 56 to 102. The further consideration of the report was then adjourned. MISCELLANEOOB.—The consideration of the Royal Courts of Justice Bill was resumed in Committee.—Sir H. GIF. FARD objected to heavy fees being inflmted on every suitor for the building of the new Law Courts.—Mr. COURTNEY defended the provisions of the bill.—Mr. INDERWICK oppo- sed the Government plan of raising the money for the Law Courts —The SoLicipon-CrENErtat defended the clause as carrying out an arrangement decided upon in 1865.—Upon a division the clause was negatived, amidst opposition cheers by 71 to 47.—Progress was reported at 2-15.—The Customs and Inland Revenue Bill was read a third time; the Sum- mary Jurisdiction Repeal, &c, Bill passed through commit- tee; the Lords' amendments to the Greek Marriage Bill were considered and agreed to ; the Contagious Diseases Animals Act (1878) Districts Bill was read a second time; the Tramways and Public Companies (Ireland) Act, 1883, Amendment Bill was read a second time.
... The House adjourned at 2-50. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TuEsnaY.

_ The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4-15. The LORD CHANCELLOR presented a bill making certain amendments in the Judicature Act, and it was read a first time. CRUELTY TO Aettetar.s.—The House went into Commit- tee on the Earl of Redesdale's Cruelty to Animals Acts (amendment No. 2) Bill, and on the motion of the Earl of MILLTOWN several amendments were inserted, one of whiCh ' provided that one of the persons visiting pigeon shooting matches to ascertain whether cruelties were practised should be a policeman.—At the instance of Earl FORTESCUE a clause was added authorising a moiety of the;fine to be paid at the discretion of the magistrate to the officer prosecuting, and the bill as amended was ordered to be reported. CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT BILL.—T,Ie Earl of DAL- HOUSIE having moved the third reading of this Bill, the Earl of LONGFORD questioned whether it was worth while to proceed further with a bill to which there were so many amendments.—The Earl of GALLOWAY suggested that the Bill should be recommitted.-1 heir lordships divided, and the third reading was carried by 101 votes to 45.—0 n the question that the Bill do pass, Lord FITZGERALD proposed, as a matter of great public policy, to rescind the amend- ment inserted in committee enabling justices to hear cases under the act in private. If the amendment were carried it would not in any way interfere with the authority inherent in the judges to exclude women and children.—Tne Earl of DAewoustE, on the part of the Government, accepted the proposal.—Lord BRAMWELL, being of opinion that it was not desirable to makespecial provision enabling judges to exclude' the public, advised the omission of the second clause alto- gether.—The Earl of DALHOUSIE consented, and the clause was struck out.—The Earl Of. WEMYSS proposed to alter from 16 to 1.5 the age at which consent could be pleaded.— The Earl of retaioustE hoped the House would adhere to the clause.—The Earl of Mira:rower supported the amend- ment, which, on a division was negatived by 70 to 58.— Lord BRABOURNE proposed the omission of the 19th clause, which authorised the police to take into custody women walking the street for an immoral purpose.—Lord MOUNT TEMPLE supported the clause, and the Archbishop of CAN- terbury considered it necessary for giving effect to the object of the bill.—A. division was taken, and the clause was re- tained by 82 votes to 43.—0 n the motion of Lord FITZ.. GERALD a clause was added declaring that it was lawful for the judge to exclude from the court whore an offence under the Act was being tried all women and all persons under 21 years of age.—A proposal by the Earl of LIMERICK to omit the 12th clause Was defeated by 49 to 15.—Clause 13 was struck out on the inotien of the LORD CHANCELLOR, and the bill passed. BILLS ADVANCED.—The Summary Jurisdiction over Chil- dren (Ireland) Bill was read a third time and passed. The Fisheries (Ireland) Bill was read a second time. The School, &c., Buildings (Ireland) Bill, and the Improvement of Lends (Ecclesiastical Benefices) Bill were read a second time. _

The House rcse at 7-35. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MESDAV. The Speaker took the chair shortly after 2-0. "DESPOTISM" IN THE SCILLY ISLES—On the motion for the third reading of the Smith's Trust Estate Bill, Mr. LABOUCHERE denounced the system of depotism in the Scilly Islands which the bill would sanction. That the sys- tem had been so far a benevolent one he did not deny, but that the house should perpetrate a system of despotism that bad existed from 1510 was a monstrous scandal, and had he any hope of success he would divide against the bill.—Sir W. HARCOURT hoped the hon. member for Northampton would be convinced that the state of facts was, under the peculiar system of tenure, wholly inconsistent with his theory. It could be wished that such a system of benevolent despotism could be exercised over some of the western Islands of Scotland.—Sir A. terwey recited the particulars of the lease to Mr. Smith, to which the Duchy of Cornwall had required Parliamentary sanction, and briefly showed how advantageous it would be to the inhabitants—Mr. JESSE COLLINGS joined in Mr. Laboucbere's protest, and thought a division should be taken.—Mr. W. H. SMITH sup- ported the bill, which was read a third time. BERBER AND KtranTeme.—la answer to Mr. A. Bartlett, the Marquis of HARTINGTON said that a battalion of British infantry had left Assiouet for Assouan. It was desirable to support the Egyptian troops and give confidence to the natives. The Government had at present no certain infor- mation as to the fate of the garrison of Berber. It was be- lieved, though not absolutely certain, that the place has either been taken or surrendered. but the report of the mas- sacre of the garrison was not confirmed. As to Khartoum, the Government had received no information since yesterday (Monday), when Major Chermside telegraphed from Sue.- kim that pilgrims had arrived there 40 days from Khartoum and 24 from Berber. They reported that Khartoum was in , the bands of the Government, and steamers coming and going. There were few Arabs between Berber and Khar- toum. He was unable to add anything to the statement al- ready made.—Mr. CHAPLIN asked if it was to be understood that the Government had made no preparations to save Khartoum.—The Marquis of HARTINGTON said that he had stated the other day that the Government had made some preparations, but that no decision as to the nature of those operations had been come to as to the construction of a rail- way between Suakim and Berber. TROOPS FOR NATAL.-1/I reply to Sir M. Hicks-Beach, Mr. ASTLEY said that the South Lancashire Regiment would embark for Natal on the 28th inst., hut not neces- sarily to reinforce the troops in Zululand. Drafts. num- bering 337 men, would also go to Natal; 300 men of the Northampton Regiment had been ordered from the Cape Colony to Natal. The Governor of Natal had been to the reserve, and they heard under date May 25th that he had decided to increase the forces in the reserve to 800. THE EGYPTIAN CONFERENCE.—Lord GEORGE HAMILTON asked whether the Great Powers had entered the Egyptian Conference on the principle that its decisions were to be in- operative unless sanctioned by the Parliament of Great R Rain ?—Mr. GLADSTONE said that the Powers had not been asked to assent to any propositions except those which had been already mentioned by the Government and printed in the papers laid before the House; but for the last four weeks it had been matter of notoriety that the proceedings of alovernment in relation to Egypt would be subject to the approval of Parliament. —ln reply to a string of questions by Lord G. Hamilton, Lord R. Churchill, Sir R. A. Cross, Mr. Chaplin, Mr. Gibson, and Mr. Heneage, Mr. GLADSTONE said answers from the other Powers as to their consent to Eng- land's proposals to France load not yet been received. There had scarcely been time. The meeting of the Conference would not be affected by those replies, its object being to discuss Egypt's financial necessities. ihe Government saw conclusive objection to their informing Parliament of their financial proposals which would, however, be dependent on the judgment of Parliament. The Government being anxious to fulfil their pledge to Parliament had made a com- munication to Parliament as soon as tbey had placed them- selves in communication with the Powers. THE FRANCHISE BILL THROUGH COMMITTEE. —ln answer to Sir W. Lawson, Mr. GLADSTONE stated that if the report on the Franchise Bill were agreed to at that sitting of the House, he should ask the House to read the bill a third time on Thursday.-On the further consideration of the report of the Representation of the People Bill, several ver- b.,l or technical amendments were proposed by the Govern- ment, and agreed to; and the bill was, amid cheers from the Liberal benches, ordered to be reprinted, and the third read- ing was fixed for Thursday. I MEDICAL ACT AMENDMeTNT MUNDELLA moved the second reading of this bill, which had already passed the House of Lords, and was, he stated, substan- tially an embodiment of recommendations of the Royal Commission of 1881, namely, uniformity of qualification, reciprocity or equal rights of practice throughout the United Kingdom, direct representation on the Medical Council, a national pharmacopma, and a medical registration for qualified practitioners.—Sir L. PLAYFAIR supported.— Col. Ktwor-Ilwator said he should not persevere with hie motion for the rejection of the bill.—Mr. BRYCE expressed a general approval of the measure, but criticised some of its details —Mr. GIBSON trusted the bill would pass with necessary amendments in committee.—Mr. J. A. CAMPBELL also approved the main objects of the bill.--Mr. GRAY viewed with apprehension the centralising tendency of the bill. In Ireland it would prove fatal to the medical corpora- tions.—The bon. member was speaking at 6.50, when, under the Standing Orders, the debate stood adjourned. The Summary Jurisdiction Repeal, ecc., Bill was considered as amended, and read a third time. The sitting was then suspended. A COUNT OTIT.—At the evening sitting at nine o'clock, Sir H. Holland waste have called attention to the state of affairs in Zululand, and to moveßa resolution, but before he could rise, attention was called to the fact that there was not a quorum, and the House was at once counted out. HOUSE OF COMMONS.--WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at half-past twelve. The Manchester Ship Canal Bill, which stood for second reading, was postponed until next day. ESTATE BILIS —Mr. A. ARNOLD proposed as a new Stand- ing Order that in the case of any Estate Bill the committee on the bill shall report specially to the House if the bill contains provisions extending either the term or the area of any settlement of land, and the report of the committee shall be printed and circulated with the votes. In many private landlills, the hon. member said, that were before the House of Lords there were matters of public interest which the House of Commons ought to know. All he asked was that that House might receive information of the same nature as that which it was necessary for the examining judges to give to the other House of Parliament-Mr. CRAIG SELLAR, in seconding the motion, urged that the proposed Standing Order would to some extent relieve the arduous labours of the Chairman of Committees.—Sir A. °TWAY considered the proposed Standing Order would be a valuable addition, and had therefore much pleasure in sanctioning it. He reminded the Ham at the same time that these bills

div.p: 111 E EXAMINER SATURDAY, JUNE 28. 1884.

Ireceived the careful and able examination of Lord Redes- dale, and of the standing counsel of both Houses. ' The motion was agreed to. The AGREEMENT WITH FRANCE.—NOTICE OF °PEON- TION.—Sir S. NoRTHCOTE—In the absence of my hon. friend the member for Portsmouth, I desire to give notice that he will, on an early day, or at the earliest oppor• tunity he can obtain, move "That the terms of the agreement entered into between her Majesty's Government and the Government of France, as indicated in the corres- Pondence recently presented to Parliament, are not such as in the opinion of this House would lead to the establishment of tranquillity and good government in Egypt—(Opposition cheers)—or justify the assumption by this country of any responsibility by way of loan or guarantee in the settlement of Egyptian finance." I also give notice that I will to-mor- row ask the Prime Minister what arrangement ha can make to give an opportunity for a discussion of that notice. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. ARNOLD intimated that when the motion just read by the right hon. gentleman is brought forward, he will move as an amendment "That this House withholds its opinion upon the result of the negotiations with France un- til it has been placed in possession of the proposals to be submitted to the Conference of the Powers of Europe upon the financial affairs of Egypt." (Ministerial cheers). THE CEMETERIES SILL.—Mr. S. Leighton and Mr. C. Read presented petitions against the Bill.—Mr. RICHARD moved its second reading The measure dealt principally with two points. One of these was the obligation imposed upon burial boards to divide new cemeteries into a conse- crated and an unconsecrated part. There was groat and growing opposition in the country to this law. All he asked was that those who believed in consecration should have it performed on their own initiative, and at their own expense; and that it should be simply an ecclesiastical pro- ceeding and carry with it no legal obligation. The other part of his Bill related to certain rights possessed by clergy- men and other ecclesiastical officers to receive in the con- secrated part of cemeteries the same fees as they received in churchyards before they were closed. The cemetery com- panies provided the ground, the labour, and the service, and the clergy had no interest in or concern with these things, but when the Cemetery Act was passing they succeeded in having their claims to compensation for loss of fees recognised, and some of those claims were simply monstrous. —Mr.RATIIBONE seconded the motion for the second reading. —Mr. BERESFORD HOPE made a lively attack upon Noncon- formists in general, and the Liberation Society in particular. The Bill was, he hotly declared, a purposeless, mischievous, provocative, and aggressive violation of a compact made fotir years ago, and he moved its rejection.—Mr. H. FOWLER protested in the strongest manner against the language used by Mr. Beresford Hope. The Bill now before the House was, he argued, a natural and legitimate consequence and development of the Act of 1880.—Mr. ELTON and Mr. A. EGERTON gave a modified opposition to the Bill, whilst Sir A. GORDON supported it —Mr. OSBORNE Mon. GAN, On the part of the Government, supported the second reading, specially approving the clauses of the Bill which provided for the abrogation of the two chapels and to the abolition of clergy- men's fees for burials in cemeteries. The Government would hold themselves free to discuss in committee various points, one being whether the Act should be retrospective. —The debate was continued by Viscount Lewisham and Mr. Hubbard, who opposed the second reading; Mr. Crop- per and Mr. Woodall, who supported the bill : Mr. Gregory, Mr. Tom Collins, Colonel Makins, and Mr. J. G. Talbot.— The House divided upon Mr. B. Hope's amendment, which was rejected by 176 votes against 15I.—The question that the bill be read a second time was then put —Mr. STANHOVE objecting, the debate necessarily stood adjourned, it being now ten minutes to six. The Licensing Act, 1872 (Amendment), Bill passed , through committee, and the House adjourned at a few min- i utes before six.

HOUSE OF LORDS—THURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter past four o'clock. In the House of Lords last evening the Earl of CARNAtt• VON gave notice of a vote of censure upon the Government in respect of the agreement with France, which he would invite the Housa to condemn as "not likely te lead to the establishment of tranquility and good order in Egypt. or to produce a result adequate to the sacrifices England has made and may be called upon to make in that country."—The bill creating a Secretary for Scotland passed through Corn- mittee, the National Debt Bill was read a second time, and after considering other and minor measures, their Lordships adjourned at twenty minutes to eight o'clock.
