div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TIIIIRSDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TIIIIRSDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. The Lords' amendments to the Stalybridge Gas Bill were considered and agreed to. THE SHIP CANAL BILL. On the order for the second reading of the Manchester I Ship Canal Bill, Mr. S. SMITH asked the House to eive its attention to the bill before passing it through that stage, and said it was the opinion of all the best authorities who had studied the matter that the works proposed to be laid down by the Canal Company in the upper estuary would inevitably silt up the 'river and destroy the navigation, thus causing a nationall calamity. In this way, Mr. Smith contended, the 800,000 people who live within five miles epf Liverpool Exchange would be ruined, the millions of money invested in docks and other property in Liverpool would be lost, and the only port on the north-west coast of England would be destroyed. Even if the canal were a success, the saving to Manchester I would be small, and its success was very problematical, and was not believed in by the best opinion even in Manchester. It was monstrous, he thought, that such great tisk should be run for so doubtful a scheme. To the canal itself Liverpool had no objection, but the scheme could be carried out with- out imperilling the navigation of the Mersey if only the route were changed for 10 or 15 miles, and he trusted that this would be ineieted upon before the bill was passed.— Mr. JACOB BRIGHT remarked that last year the bill had been pas ed by a committee of the Commons and this year by the Lou is, and that Manchester was as much interested in maintaining the navigability of the Mersey, as was Liver- pool. He thought that with the aid of Manchester the I navigation could be improved and the Mersey made a har- bour refmge. As to the Liverpool docks they were of a most antiquated character, without connection with the railways or modern facilities, and Liverpool was the dearest port in the country. He was as much in favour of the appoint- ment of a strong committee as Mr. Smith.—Mr. HOULDS- WORTH supported Mr. Bright's views, and Mr. ARNOLD followed upon the same side.—Then Mr. W. RATHBoNE supplemented Mr. Smith's arguments, dwelling on the fact that there was no objection to a canal to Manchester, which might, perhaps, benefit Liverpool, but there was a tremend- ous danger of the creation of new sandbanks.—Mr. Slagg, Sir A. Otwav, and Mr. Balfour said a few words, after which Sir J. MOWBRAY assured the House that the strongest possi- ble committee should be selected to consider the bill.—Mr. Whitley, Mr. Maclver, and Mr. Hicks then joined in the de- bate,and the bill was read a second time. QUESTIONS —THE VOTE OF CENSTIRE.—At question time, Lord E. FITZILLURICE announced the abandonment sf the Congo Treaty, hut said a new treaty would be negotiated to establish a river commission like the Danubian Commission In the course of his replies to a number of question as to the Conference, Mr. GLADSTONE said that all the Powers, including the Porte, had agreed to attend, but it was doubt- ful if Tarkey would be represented at the first meeting, the date of which could not, owing to the condition of the finan- ces of Egypt, be delayed. The Premier also announced that the debate on the vote of censure should begin on Monday. THE FRANCHISE BILL.—THIRD READING PASSED. In moving the third reading of the Franchise Bill, Mr. GLADSTONE asked if a small bill like this took so long to pass what would have been the prospect if the Government had joined redistribution with it. It would have been well nigh impossible for a Redistribution Bill to have received the Royal assent, and for the Government to have united redistribution with the franchise in the same measure would have been a fraud upon the House and the country. The Government had done everything to avoid a quarrel with the House of Lords, a quarrel which the Government would regard as a calamity of the greatest importance to the coun- try, a calamity bringing into question the Parliamentary ' institutions under which we had lived so long, a conflict which would be acceptable to men of revolutionary opinions, but which it was the solemn duty of the Government to use all reasonable means to avoid. Hence the Government had taken the most moderate course at the risk of offending some of their most generous and trusted supporters. The probability of such a conflict between the two Houses he deemed to be the most serious crisis in his recollection since the crisis of the corn laws. He would not put a limit to the mischief and difficulties that would result, but most grave he was confident they would be. What the issue would be be had no doubt.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE said the speech of Mr. Gladstone was an ex- traordinary one—not upon the merits of the bill but as to whether the House of Lords was any longer to form a Par- liament, whether it was to take any part in legislative work, or whether it was to be bound by the will of a majority of the House of Commons, or even the will of an imperious Minister. Was the House of Com- mons bound to listen to these threats, and, daunted by them, to refuse to do the duty that lay upon them? It was not the duty of the House of Com- mons to discuss lhe Mine that the Lords would take, but Mr. Gladstone came forward and in a most theatrical man- ner made threats, the meaning of which it was impos- sible to misunderstand. Sir Stafford Northcote went on to contend that the measure was a very incomplete one, and that the House had never been told what the Govern- ment had been driving at.—Mr. GOSCHEN said be had op- posed the bill because be was against the vital principle of it. It appeared to him that the time for further opposition to the principle of the suffrage had passed away. He had therefore made his last speech against it, and should look forward to the question ,of redistribution to see that there was a fair and equitable distribu- tion of political power.—After considerable debate, The SPEAKER at 20 minutes past eight, put the question that the bill be read a third time, and there being no cries Of "no" in response to the "ayes," declared that the " ayes " had it. Loud and prolonged cheers followed this declaration.—Mr. GLADSTONE: I desire to observe that the bill has been read a third time nemine contradicente. (Hear, hear.) I trust it will be se recorded.—The SPEAKER repeated the words of Mr. Gladstone that the bill had been ' read a third time remise contradicente, and the Clerk at the table so recorded it arsid renewed cheering. The Medical Ameniment Bill was read a second time,and the House afterwards went into Committee OR the Hours of Polling Bill. The House adjoarned at five minutes past three o'clock in the morning.

SATURDAY, JUNE 28, 1884.

HER MAJESTY'S Opposition seem to be doomed to disappointment. The oppor- tunity of overthrowing the Government is, according to their showing, always at hand, but somehow nothing ever comes of it. The Conservatives were confident when Mr. GLAD- STONE was called upon to take the place of Lord BEACONSFIELD that the Liberals would not be able to hold together for six months, but it is getting well on towards six years, and they stand as well before the country to-day as they did when they first took office. The codes have been deluding themselves with the superstition that because the present Ministry had set themselves upon reform at home they would be sure to blunder in their policy abroad. "The wish was father to the thought ;" but wishing will not remove a Prime Minister, or Mr. GLADSIONE would have disappeared long ago. Egypt, in the opinion of the Opposition, is the vulnerable point in the Liberal armour. The other day it was in relation to General GORDON ; but the attack in that direction has failed again and again. This time it is the agreement with France as to future action in Egypt ; and a cock-and-bull story as to how the Government had surrendered everything to our neighbour having been invented by a Metropolitan journal, the Tories were in high glee at the proposal of " another vote of censure," which should, of course, end in a Government defeat and a dissolution. There was such a stir in London as was quite puz- zling to us simple-minded people in the coun- try who are anxious chiefly about the fate of the Franchise Bill, and are quite content to trust complicated details of foreign policy to the PRIME MINISTER'S skill, foresight, and innate sense of justice. But the Opposi- tion thought otherwise; the chancelad come to them; and they crowded the House of Commons on Monday evening to be ready to make the most of it. Mr. GLA.DSTONE, the p fidious representative of " perfidious Albion," was to give an account of the pro- posed agreement between England and France ; he was to confess his manifold sins and iniquities; and then the Tories would execute him on the spot. A very interesting programme from the Conservative point of view, but unfortunately for them it was not carried out. They found that the Government had not done anything so silly as they had been led to expect ; and they were for the moment thrown on their beam-ends. Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE,WhO is always discreet if not always valiant, contented himself with a mild sort of ptotest, coupled with the sug- gestion that a vote of censure would be forth- coming when the leaders of the party had taken time to consider the official papers. This was not sufficient for the wild spirit of Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL; he is one of those who rush in where angels fear to tread. He flourished the tomahawk in this instance in a lively style, but when he had finished it was perceived that nobo ly had been scalped. The cheers with which the Liberal members of the House of Commons received Mr. GrAosTrinit's statement uf the terms of agree- ment with France showed that if ever any of them had had any doubts on the subject,

The law as to Trades Unions has been grad- ually cleared of objectionable features; but it is still far from perfect as was seen from a case tried at Salford on Wednesday A mem- ber of the Amalgamated Society of Engineers, named Collinge, sued the Society for the sum of Erg tBs. to which, he alleged, he was en- titled under the rules' as allowance, he having been out of work over twelve months. No question was raised as to the correctness of the sum claimed, but it was explained that Collinge, who joined the organisation in 1867, was excluded in 188 z for acting contrary to the interests of the Society. His offence was that, during a certain strike, he remained "in " with non-union men. The defence was that Mr. Jordan, who sat as judge, had no jurisdiction in the matter, the " Trades Union Act, 1871," leaving such organisa- tions outside the pale of the law. The ob- ject of the act was to relieve Trades Unions of the liability of being dealt with for conspiracy, but at the same time the law refused its sanction to rules which went in he direction of interfering with and restraining trade. Mr. JoRDAN seems to have been somewhat irritated at finding that, from the state of the law, he must give a verdict for the defendants. On the solicitor for the defence urging that it was not an illegal society, the Judge replied: "I think you are an i legal society, and banded together for an illegal purpose, and I am astonished at you showing your heads in a court of law before judge and jury." He further showed his feeling in the matter by refusing costs to the defendants. Now, it is no doubt hard for a man who has regularly paid into a society for fifteen years to find that he is shut out, and mat he cannot claim the protection of the law. But it is tolerably well known amongst Trade Unionists that they go beyond what the law is prepared to sanction in the stringency of their trade regulations; and there are few, we should think, who are not aware that they cannot take their rules into court if 'anything goes wrong. At any rate, a person who joins the Amalgamated Society of Engineers has the opporiunity of reading the rules, and if he does not like the power of exclusion which is given under them he need not remain a member. If he is anxious to obtain high wages as the result of the pressure which a strong society can always bring to bear-- a pressure which is not countenanced by the law—he should on the other hand be willing to take the risk of such a connection. It is not denied that Collinge broke the very rules under which he claimed his allowance, and having once submitted himself to the Society it seems to us he ought to be bound by its regulations. This does not of course touch the question as to whether it is wise to join societies that a Judge may describe as "ille- gal." Still they are in existence, and, speak- ing of them as a whole, they are doing such good work that we cannot but think the wisest course would be to go a step further And open the door to those of them that are desirous of obtaining, with a modification of their rules, the sanction and shelter of the law. The anomaly is sufficiently glaring and ought to be removed.

Not that there was no opposition. N3body doubts that if the making of the Canal should lead to the silting up of the river it would be a calamity; but there are competent engineers Who say there need be no fear of silting, Itnd,. if capitalists care to incur the risks ofl the undertaking, having . all the elements of the problem before them, it cannot be re- garded. as an unreasonable thing to permit them to make the attempt to carry it out. It waS stated in the course of the debate that the tall had not evoked much popular entho- slam. This may be true as to Liverpool, but it is not true as to Manchester, nor as to Warrington. The Town's Meetingin the Public Ilan on Thursday evening was crowded to excess, and those who were present were prac- ticing unanimous in supporting the scheme. l'he feeling of the inhabitants all along the line of the river is that the construction of the canal will be a good thing for them; five Millions of money cannot be spent without some of it finding its,way into 'their pockets, and they are quite wide.awake, if not Wholly disinterested, in their expression of opinion. Whether they will be disposed to carry their support so far as to find Money to any large extent for carrying out the underta,king is another thing. It is, in our judgment, a matter for the large capitalists rather than the small investors, and working-men will do well, therefore, to look before they map when it comes to a question of investment. It doesn't do to put all one's eggs in one basket, and those only Should be placed in the big basket of the Ship Canal which can be well spred if the Worst comes to the worst. There is always Plenty of capital in this country ready to be turned into what may be deemed an ultimately' Profitable channel. What is asked is that authority ,should be given to allow it to flow into the Ship Canal scheme. , Manchester asks for no more and, after the pledges given, she has a right to say she will be content with no less.

YOUNG RUFFIANS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty See- alone On Wednesday, before Mr. W. D. ?Jolt and Mr. H. Gas- kell junior, Patrick Burns, 13 yearsof age,and John McCabe, 12 years of age, Timperlev-street, were brought up in cus- tody charged with assaulting two ladies of good position in Farnworth. James Priestly (14), and Edward Douglas (7), deposed teethe prisoners meeting the ladies in a lane leading to learnworth, on Monday, and acting in an indecent man- ner to them. with the object of obtaining somb money. They also used bad language.— Superintendent Barker said McCabe was a very bad lad; and had been sent to gaol for sleeping out, and had received six strokes with the birch rod for thieving. There was nothing against Burns.—Mr. Holt said this was a very serious case of annoying ladies with the object of extorting money from them, and each prisoner! would be sent to gaol 21. days with hard labour. Tam BY A BARBER AT WIDNES —At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Joseph Davies, a respectable look- ing young fellow, was charged with steeling a whetstone, a pair of pincers, two spoons, ter.," sugar crushers, and a ptir of curling ;nags, the property of John Stringer, hairdresser, Widnes-road. The prosecutor said the prisoner had been in his emp/ey seven or eight weeks. On the Bth instant the articles mentioned were seta, but they were missed on Thursday, the 19th June. He asked the prisoner for them, but he stated he knew nothing about them. The articles were worth 123 61, and the prisoner had no right to take them.—John Findley, hairdresser, Midwood-street, depesed that on the 18th inst. the prisoner sold him the arric'es for half a crown.— the prisoner, who was apprehended by P.C. Tbistleton, informed the Bench that it was a drunken freak, - and alleged that Stringer was along with him—The Bench teok a lenient view ef the case, and fined the prisoner 101 an I costa. A WOMAN'S REVENGE AT WIDNES —Before Mr. W. D. Holt and Mr. H. Gaekell, junior, at Widnes, Petty'Sessiens on Wednesday, Catharine O'Toole, a married woman, was brought up under a warrant charged with threatening to assault William Patin, prevision dealer, Ann-street, and also with damaging his .property by breaking windows to the value of 7s. From the evidence of Mr. Patin and his'imice, Beteeydralin, it appeared that on Friday last the County Court baliffs executed a warrant upon the prisoner for a debt owing to Mr. PalM.' About dinner time the prisoner went to his shop and sent three stonee through the windows, and she then used mach had languegi, and threateged to take Mr. ,Palin's life. For the wilful damage the prisoner was fined is and costs 43, and ordered to pay the demege. On the other charge, the prisoner was bound over to keep the peace for three months, herself in £lO and one surely of £5, or in defeult 14 days imprisonment. The prisoner said Mr. PAM had robbed her and she. wouldn't pay him a far- thing, she would go to gaol. , CHARGES AGAINST WESTON GROCERS —At Runcorn Petty Sessions, en Monday, before Mr, W. Bankr and Mr. Charles Reynolds, John Hughes, provision dealer, Weston, was charged with having in his possession for use of trade a pair of scales which were unjust. Mrs. Hughes appeared, Superintendent Leah said On the 18th instant he visited the deferelant'inshop at Weston Point, and found a lafge scale used for weighing flour with a- 1 irge quantity of flour adhering. They were when tested 8 ouncte against the pun, t chaser. He asked Mrs. Hughes to clean the scales, which being done they were still upwards of 6 ounces against the purchaser. Mrs. Heuthes told him that they did not use the scale except to carry flour- from the warehouse, but there was no other scale in the shop for weighing Ileur ; and no other scale upon the beam. Mrs. Hughes Wormed the Bench that the scale was used for carrying flaur into the bakehonee and never for weighing. A fine of 103 and costs 9s 6cl was imposed.—A similar penalty was imposed upon Samuel Bennett, of Weston, for haying in his possession for use for trade, on the 18th instant, two weights which were not stamped as rcetaired by the Weights and Meesures Act, 1878. Superintendent, Leah observed that in addition to being unstamped they were each a drachm too light. Seamus ROBBERY BY BOYS AT RUNCORN.—Before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. Chas. Reynolds at Runcorn Petty Ses- sions on Monday, James Molyneaux (12), Samuel Lydiete (14), and Charles Edwari Miller (12), were brought up on remand charged with baying on the 20th June, etolen £l3 18e 6d, the mealier; of John Wood, a labourer in the employ of Messrs. Gossage at Widnes. They were further charged with receiving the money, knowing it to hare been stolen. It appeared that for several days Molyneaux, whose parents live in York-street, a few doors from the prosecutes house, bad keen making extensive purohatles in cricket niateriel, fiehing tackle, knives, tobacco, dm, and this caused Wood's Sister, who keeps house for him, to remark that it was very strange where Molyneaux was getting all these things from. Wood said be must have got the money from somewhere where he shenld not, and immediately went upetaire and ex- amined the iron box where he kept his cash. He found that it contained'only £3 if 61, whereas a fortnight before it had captained £l7. Suspecting the prisoner Molyneaux,. he fetched him in the house and accused him of the theft, hot he stoutly denied his guilt. Subsequently the same evening the prisoner admitted that be had entered Wood's house by means of the key of his father's house, and stolen th.to money which he had hidden under the pigeon cote in his Where's yard. Wood accompanied the prisoner to his father's yard, where he broil& £5 12e 61, wrapped in paper from beneath the cote.—The prisoner's father advised Wood to give him into custody, and the same evening P.C. Kelly took him into custody. Molyneaux then made statements incriinfhating Miller and Lydiate who were then arrested. He stated that be had 'given Lydiate £5, and Miller £3 of the stolen money' but these boys each allez,ed that Moly- neaux told them he had found a bank book in Duke's Field, and he had got it changed for £l5 —When formally charged Molyneaux pleaded guilty, but Lydiate and Miller pleaded not guilty. As MillyneauX and Lydiate had previeusly been before the court, they were each sentenced to receive 12 strokes with the birch rod, and be imprisoned three days.' Miller, who made his first appearance, was ordered to re- ceive six strokes with the lurch rod, and be imprisoned three days. ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN BAILIFF.—At Rancorw Petty Sessions, on Monday, Richard Deakin, a labouring man, was brought up under a warrant charged with having, on the 19th June, assaulted Samuel Melted, an officer of the Run- corn County Court, whilst in the execution of his duty.— The prisoner pleaded not guilty —.Mr. Burton appeared to prosecute on behalf of the High Bailiff, and stated that this offence of assaulting the Wit& of the County Court was becoming very common in the town, and be was instructed to press for a heavy penalty in this case. 'Filen officers were entitled to the protection of the law, because they had to perform a disagreeable duty put upon them by the law, and it was necessary that they should carry it out without fear.—Samuel Mailed said he was a bailiff at Runcorn County Court. On Thursday afternoon he saw the prisoner near Delph Bridge, and told him he had a commitment for him, and that he would either have to pay £2 de lid or go to gaol for 40 days. He said -he should not pay, and witness was taking hold of him, when he struck hini twice on the. breast. He went with him to Ashworth's-row, still keeping hold of him and here the prisoner trip- ped him up, and he fell upon his back. The prisoner then ran away, but left his coat behind. He (wit- ness was not much hurt. He had arrested the prisoner twice before, and knew the prisoner well —The prisoner denied that the warrant was ever read over to him, and also that he struck the bailiff.—George Torrie, bailiff at the County Court, deposed to seeing Mallad, his assistant, im- mediately after the assault had been committed. He was then covered with sand and dust.—Tae prisoner called Scsannah Raftery, who alleged that the bailiff released the prisoner, who then ran away. The prisoner did, not strike thebeiliff near her house in Ashworth's-row.—Mr. W. Bankes (chairman) said the Bench were quite satisfied the charge had been proved. He ought to know better than assault an officer in the execution °Chia duty; and he would be fined 40s and coats. He trusted this would be an example and a warning to the prisoner and others —Mr. Burton asked that the advocate's fee should be allowed—The Bench granted the application, but reduced the fine to 303 and costs, £1 6e Bd, or a month's hard labour.—The prisoner: I will go for the month. SAVAGE ATTACE ON A WIDNES PoDucAN.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Thomas McGirl. Eleanor- street, a young man, was summoned to answer a sharge of refusing to quit the Millti.tid Inn, Appleton,twhen requested to do so by the landlord George Holding, better known as Fowler.—The complainant said on the evening of the 14th inst. be found the defendant sitting on the kitchen table, and eeveral other men round about him. In consequence of previous annoyances he had received from this man, he had forbidden him to enter the house; and on this evening when passing him the defendant kicked him en the leg and asked him if he knew him. Witness replied that he did, and did not wish to receive any insults from him. He also in- I formed him that if he did not go out he should put him I out, whereupon the defendant with an oath defied him. , Witness then put the defendant out three times. The de- I fendant pulled off his coat and hat and challenged him to 1 fight, and be and his companions commenced an attack upon him.—ln answer to Mr. Knowles, witness said on one evening ' the defendant and his companions threw about 400 stones into the racing track of the recreation grounds when the runners were practicing. To frighten them he fired two blank cartridges at them.—Miss Faunton, barmaid, gave corroborative evidence.—The defendant was called, and said he asked complainant why he shot at him. The complain- ant thereupon seized him by the throat and " thumped " him, and but for a companion to his aid, he would have been iniared. Complainant fetched a revelver to him. AI week previously the complainant shot him four times and ha fell down. He could not leave the hones when the corn- plainent had bold of his throat---Patrick.Newall, of Dixon- street, and Thomas Kelly gave Corroborative testimony.— McGirl and Newell were than charged with assaulting Hold- ing. The complainant alleged that he put McGirl out of the house no less than three times. On the fourth time of entering the house McGiri reized bin by the arm of his woollen jacket which he nearly tore out, tore his collar off, and pulled his cuff off. He lost a sleeve-link worth 7s. 6d. Altogether there were five young men surrounding hint, some kicked at him, others struck at him with their fists, and attempted to drag him out of the house. McGirl and Newell each kicked and struck him. He had a big lump on one side of his head and another on the back of his head. Mies Taunton, the barmaid, was naming to his assistance, when Neelall ran at her with his head, knocking her against the wall. He also struck her on the side of the head with his fist, and almost rendered her insensible with his violence. Witness called out for his life preserver, and whilst it was being brought to him, the defendants and their campanions ran out. He had to Call for the preserver for his own pre- tection becalms be was set upon by a band of young ruffians. —Miss Taunton confirmed this statement. —The defence was a direct denial of the charge.—Mr. Holt said this was a very serious case of assaulting a licensed victualler whilst preserving order in his hones, and each of the efendante ivonld be fined 56 and costs 103 81, or seven days' imprison- ment for the assault. For the more serious offence of refus- ing to quit Melte was fined las and costs, or 14 days.

The fortnightly meeting WA% held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, 4r. J. Weir presiding. There were present Messrs. Mclntyre, Derbyshire, Alidwood, Wallington, Aaron, H. Linaker (clerk), W. U. Linaker (deputy clerk), and Far. • 110gt(111 in4pector ). • THE FRYER OUTBREAK AT SUTTON.—Dr. Adams, the offie,e, reported I hat Mrs. Margaret Woodior, aged 59 years, residing at a hause situated between Preston, Brook and Sutton village had oeen attacked with typhoki fever. l'he facts of the case were consistent with the by- potnesis that the water supply of Taylor's pump had been the immediate amu!ce,of infection. Thomas Edward Savage,' ,geii seven years, died from typhoid fever ou the 21st inst. l'his was the only victim of the ou,break tip to the present 'line. Since the last rep wt all pas.dhle sanitary precautions had been taken that lay in their power, and house to hottse Yieltati'm mole by the inspec'or and himself, and he was now able to express his expectation that the ,outbreak was

; arrested.--A short discussion took place upon the drainage • and water supply of Sutton, and the further consideration of the matter was ildjaurned until the next meeting, it being understood that the clerk and the inspector would do all that was necessary in the meantime.—lt was decidel that a bill of £24 4s 3.1 from M. el. Bancroft for inspecting springs, dice in January and February, 183, with reference to Sutton water supply, be paid. FRoDsliAlif WATER SUPPLY.—The minutes of the Frod- sham Perochial,Corntnitree which were adopted, contained the following repart from Mr. Henry Bancroft, the In- quirer :—" In accordance with 'your instructions, I be to , report that met Mr. It 'ben Ashton and Mr. Farrington at Five Crossea on the 11th inst. We inspected the lend on the westerly side of the highway between Newton Hall end Springside, and selected a site for sinking a trial well. From the contour and general appearance of the land, and also from information we received on the spot. I have every reason to believe that water can be met with at probably from four to six yards bedew the surface of the ground. rat once wrote to Mr. flitchen; the solicitor to the tremors of the late Major ilitchen, and have made the following arrangements with him, viz :—That he allows a trial well to be sunk pro- viding the Authority pays for all surface damage; that the well is either to be filled up and the surface restored to its original condition or left open at the option of the trustees; : that the Authority is to fix a temporary fence and to be re-5 sponsible for any accident during tho time they are in pos- session; and that I am to meet him on the ground and point out the exact position where it is proposed to sink. On the enclosed tracing I have shown the place where the well, in my opinion, should be. It may hereafter be necessary to drive edits or levels over the part coloured red to bring all the water to a focus. After the well is sunk arrangements should be made for continuous pumping for a few days to ascertain its yield, and the water should be analyzed, as , I understand the water in the well at New- ton Hall has been seriously injured by a gaso- meter being placed 'near R. Hitchen was \ unable' to quote a price, as be did not quite understand un- til he called here to-day wbat the Authority wanted, but he assured nee the trustees would not be unreasonable. Pro. viling the well turns out satisfactory, and water is found at the depth I anticipate, no perneenent pumping will be re- quired. If water was taken from this source the cost of the scheme would be about the same as if it was obtained from Mr. Wriehtes laud; but I presurn• there would be no riparian owners to comperoene. I have also c)nsidered the sugges- tion t 4 sink a well near the Gas Works cm Frodshatin Marsh, and lift the water. The lift to the proposed service reservoir I , would b 3 142 feet, and to Five Crosses 261. feet. The level of the ground about the Cras Works is only 20 feet above , ordnance datum, which is about the level of an extraor- dinary spring tide. I don't know if any analysis has been, made of the water, but I should be very dubious about its (lenity. There is not, in my opinion, sutficient water power anywhere about the mush or in the town to lift, the water either to Five Crosses or to the reservoir the simplest plan would be to work a steam pump, from a large boiler, or I , have a double acting pump in connection with an engine, and by an arraneernent of valves force the water either into the tower or upper reservoirs. If this scheme was adopted either two small reservoirs would be required, one in Fluin- lane and the other at Five Crosses, or duplicate boilers, pumps, and rising trains would be necessary, else the district would be without a water supply shook! an accident occur,, and with such considerable lifts this might be very fre- event. My estimate for this scheme amounts to £10,689. When I was at Fwdshatn on the 11th inst., I met the Chairman, and it was arranged that I sheuld eeein tont ipeeelf int 9 wriungqicttiOn with Mr. Stretch, and eek him and his co-leustee to te-temesider their proposal, as the committee considered teetir terms very excessive. In reply Mr: Knowles Stretch writes me I have to acknowledge yours of the 12'h instant, and will zee Mr. Warrington on his return to town next week.' Mr. Farring- ton has drawn my attention to another spring. He writes on the 14th :—' I was at Helsby yesterday, and met with' what lam informed is a never failing spring of water. It is situate in a field on the lower aide of. lieleby village off troiu and below the railway station. It comes to the sur- face, and is at present passing through a kind of stone trough, in which there is a slot two inches wide, sad the water is running one inch deep through such slot. I find that the water is much used by the inhabitants, and have obtained a sample and intend to submit the acme for analy- sis.' It there is only one inch flowing over a two inch slat it is not sufficient for your diet:let ; besides the spring is at too low a level for a gravitation scheme. If you decide upon sinking the tidal well, I would recommend you to ask Mr. Littler, or some other contraczor, his terms for doing it. It should be six feet in diameter. 3he brickwork must rest on a curb or flat ring made of oak or elm, four inches thick, and its breadth should be the full thickness at the lining. It ought to be made in two layers, breaking joint and well emitted tegether. Toe brickwork should be nine inches thick and laid dry for the first four feet from the bottom; above that level it ought to be set in hydraulic mortar to prevent any surface watergetting in. I would also adviseyoutoobtain terms for the pumping, including treepess and all cantingen- eke." The committee recommended' that Mr. Bancroft's suggestion to sink a trial well be carried out, and the Clerk was directed to obtain tenders for the work ,from Mr. Tim- mine, of Runcorn, and Mr. Littler, of Five Crosses.

The monthly meeting was held on Thursday', Mr. Brad- shaw, the vice-chair:nen, presiding. There were present MesArs. Brock, i,eacou, Glover, Davies, and Danby (clerk). DISTRICV EDUCATION COMMITTEE. —The minutes of this, committee stated that during the month of May there were 50 applications for the paym.nt of school fe?s, which were recommended to be paid io 45 cases; end 234 persons ap- peared before the committee for contravention of the Educa- tion Act. Thirty-three persons were brought before the magistrates and convicted and one boy was sent to an indus- trial school. It was recommended that the seal of the Board be affixed to the agreement with the managers of the Indus- trial training ship S' Clio," for the reception of children com- mitted under the 14th or 15th sections of the Industrial choals Act, 1866, by a magistrate's warrant, upon the ap- plication er with the sanction of this Board, in con- sideration of a payment by this Board at the rate of 2s per week towards the maintenance during the period of lite detention of each child committed; also a contribution of Sc per week for every boy committed tinder the ,1.13 th section of Induitrial Schools Act, 1868. and under sections of Elementary Education Act, 1878.— In moving the adoption of the minutes, Mr. Deacon ex- I .plained that the Board now pilaf the managers of the "Clio" is 61. per week towards the maintenance of atop, but they now asked for 2s. per week, and the Board would either have to pay that amount or not send boys to that ship. Of course they should not send boys to the training sbipaniless there was some speclal reason. The Board bad 46 boys in industrial schools, and out of that numbs: only two were on the" Clio."—The minutes were passed.

VISIT ,TO TEE INDUSTRIAL SCNOOLS.-14r. Deacon gave an account of a visit which the District Education Com- mittee had paid to the children who were in Ic.dustrial Schools. He observed that they found that some schools were bettor than others, although it was impossible to judge simply from a stray visit, but no thought he ought to men- thol that St. George's School stood .at the top a the list. Tho arrangements there seemed extremely good, and the place looked beautifully clean and very comfortable. With the exception of one boy in Beacon-Moe School all the boys were in good health, and they seemed to be satisfactory in 111 respects —The ChairmarFsaid the Board wovld be glad to hear Bluth a satisfactory accouht of their Industrial Schools, and their thanks were due to the cosEmittee for their visit. _

Gunning be arpointed as- sistant mistress in the junior girl' trtment oi the Simnes Cross schools., three menthe on trial (vice Mies Urquhart) at a salary of £35 pr annum, and if found efficient, then to rise abccordiag to the ,SCile of the Riard. Recommended that Miss Strickland's engagement terminate immediately after the (i.orernment ex imination in September next, in- stead of July 31st, ISM. The comrnitteereported that caretaker Hughes, of Simirr's Cross schools died on the 11th instant; and recommended that his widow. M. A. The late Mr. Stitt ing'Crawford, alt hough he had a dowager duchess to wife, was understood not to lead a life of un- cheoquered joy. He bad one resource which soothed him in his dullest reorients. This was hie cigar room, where be had stored what he bustled et as the largest and best stook out of the trade. He never let it run below ten thousand, and if he heard anywhere of a choice parcel that was to be had for money -he did not mind going high above his mini- mum stock. It was irreverently stid by one of his friends "when he died, that " it was a great blessing Stirling Craw- ford could not take his cigaro with him. They would be burned at both -ends." What was to become of the famous -stock has long been a matter of anxious inquiry. It Was known that the Duchess of Montrose could not smoke them 'herself, and it was believed that she was not likely to sub- divide them for presents among the old companions of her ',late husband. It is now understood that they are lobe sold by auction, a report that has excited as much interest among connoisseurs of cigars as the dispersal of the Fountains col- lection or the sale of the Leigh Court Gallery has created in art circles. Never within the memory of man has so large a collection of the choicest brands of the best growths -of cigars come upon the ,market. A new quarry of facts, arguments, and illustrations is about to be opened up for the benefit of the vast army ef E,ocial reformers who are engard in the battle against in- temperance. Within the next few days will he published a new book of reference quaintly entitled "The Foundation of Death : a Study of the Drink Question." The compiler is Mr. Axel Gurstafson, a gentleman of Swedish nationality, ' who has graduated ler some years in Enelish and Ameri- can journal ism awl literature. He has devoted an enormous amount of Hine to the'eompilation of this book, witch is a key to all knowledge hidden in all languages and all litera- ture in the matter of /drinking alcohol. Whole libraries might be filled with boeks on this subject; bat there is no comprehensive reference for it in a storehouse of facts such 1 ae Mr. Gustafson has slowly built up. The return to early fashions is a matter of yearly occur- rence. Being the other night at dinner with a well-known American sciertist, I learned with some astoniohment of 1 what I venture to believe is a generally unsuspecred revival of an elder fashion. The earliest writing in the world was done on the barks of treee. Now, with the march of science, we have returned to the tree as writing material, and ip our note paper and newspaper entertain wood unawares. Ac- cording to my informant, from fifty to seventy, per cent of ordinary American newspapers ie composed of wood. Ground cn a revolving SIORP, spruce and poplar are reduced to a form in which, with a slight addition of rage, a material excellently suited for newspaper is produced. I don't know whether it is used in this country, bet according to my in- formant it is the chief material of the American journals. Even wood is now threatened by a new rival. There is a material called bagasse which is the refuse of a sugar cane. The Great Eastern is still eating her head off, incurrinr annual charges of over £2,000 and bringing in a revenue the principle item in which is £24 received as fees from vinitors, to whom the monster ship remains an object of curiosity. Every year suggestions are made for the em- nloyment of the vessel, but they generally come to nothing. Just now, 1 hear, the directors have before thorn a proposal to send the ship out to New Orleans during the period of the Exhioidon, and tit her up as a floating hotel. With One brief gleam of success whilst engag,d in laying the Allsntle cable, the Great Eastern has been a coastant drain upon the purses of unfortuna! a shareholders. She began her career amid the thunder of the explosion which almost wrecked her OR her trial off Hastings in the autumn of 1559, and if it had closed then it would have been a good thing for many people.

EARLESTOWN. GOSPEL MissioN.—A very enjoyable entertainment in connection with the Earlestown Gospel Mission, was held in the Co-operative Hall, liege-street, on Tuesday evening, when there was a Leif lv good attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. John Clarke. A selection of recitetions, melodies, &c., was much appreciated. SAD ACCIDENT TO A STRIKER —On Wednesday forenoon Joseph Stacey, employed as a striker at the Vulcan iron foundry, met with a sad accident. Ile was momentarily engaged in removing an iron "dog" from under a fire-box casing, when the latter fell upon his right hand, smashing two of his fiegers. Stacey lost a large quantity of blood. VIADUCT WORMS Excuestows.—The annual excursions in connection wide the Viaduct Institute and waggon works belonging, to the London and North-Western Railway COM- I party will take place on Saturday, the 19th July. As ini former years special cheap trips will be run to two places of interest for one or three days—the destinations this year being London and Carnarvon. MORE ANTI-VACCINATION SoeferoNses.—Daring the pre- sent week several persons have had summonses served upon them for refusing to have their children vaccinated, and the cases will be heard at the Petty Sessions to be held at the Newton Town Hall to-morrow (Seturday). We understand that the local anti-vaccinators have engaged Mr. Thomas Duslenry, of Blackburn, to appear cn their behalf. THE EARLESTOWN CHURCH DISPUIE —The condition of off tire at the Church of St. John the Baptist, Earlestown, still remains in an unsatisfactory condition. There was little improvement, if any, in the attendance at either of the ser- vices on Sunday, though in the evening there was a slightly increased attendance owing to an attraction in the presence of the "singing pilgrims," who had given a service of song in the schoolroom in the afternoon. The preacher on both occasions was the vicar (the Rev. T. R. Matthews). Mr. A. Ilenshaw read the lessons, and Mr. Pemberton again pre- sided at the organ. The old organist (Mr. H. J. Darman) and the members of the late choir again absented them- selves. TEE " SINGING PILORIMS."—On Sunday afternoon four " singing pilgrims," announced as "ex-slaves," gave a sarvice of song in Sr. Johe'..e School. There was not a very large attendance, but these present highly appreciated thel "service." The " pilgrims " attended the service in the church on Sunday evening, and sang in the course of the service. On Menday evening a lecture on " Scene, in Slaveland " Was given in the schoolroom by one of the "ex- slaves." The chair was occupied by the vicar of the parish (the Rev. T. R. Matthews), and about 30 persons were present. The lecture was an interesting description of the social and religious life of slavery daye, of how the negroes were bought and sold as slaves, and of the cruelties and sufferings they experienced. THE NEW PRIMITIVE METHODIST SCHOOLS.—The work of erecting the new schools in cerenecion with the Primi- tive Methodist Chapel and Schools in Legh-street, Earles- town, is being proceeded with. The contract has been let to Mr. Pennington, of Earlestown, who named £705 as the amount for the work. Ire addition to this sum, however, there will be " extras " for fitting and furnishing the school. The school is being erected on a plot of land behind the present chapel and school, and the large room will accom- modate about 500 persons, while in addition there will be five class-rooms and an infants' school-room The want of more school accommodation has been long felt. The com- mencement of the erection of the building will be corn-1 memorated by the ceremony of laying "memorial stones "'I next Saturday. SEQUEL TO NEWTON RACES: OVERLOADING A TRIM law.—An extraordinary case of overloading a tramcar was heard at the St. Helens Town Hall on Monday. before Mr. A. Sinclair and Aldermen Mcßryde. Michael Logan, in the employ of the St. Helens and District Tramways CompanY, as a conductor of a tramcar, was summoned for unlawfully conveying upon a tramcar a greater number of passengers than the said tramcar Was licensed to carry, contrary to the regulations of the local anthority.--The defendant acknow- ledged the offence, but said the tramcar was started contrary to his will.—lnspector Keighley said that at ten minutes to five on the previous ffednesday afternoon he saw the de- fendant conducting No. 7 tramcar in Park-road, Parr. See- ing that he had a great load on the car he counted the num- ber of passengers, and found 31 outside and 32 inside, , making a total of 66. The car was licensed to carry 16 inside and 16 outside. There were 34 passengers too many. ; —The Chairman: Were they coming from the races ? Inspector Keighley : Yes, air. He said he told the mana- ger that he would not be responsible for the tramcar starting so crowded—Defendant: It was against my will that it started from the terminus. I told the manager that I would not be resoonsible for it if it started.—The Bench imposed a tine of lOs and costs. DISCUSSION ON GOOD TESIPLARISZL—A meeting in con- nection with the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Lodge-room, Bridge-street, on Monday evening, when there was a large ateendance, and Bro. Geo. E. Warburton, W.C.T., presided. The programme for the evening we headed "Question Box," and a number of questions came up for discussion. Among the most im- portant were "How can we improve our lodge meetings?" "How can we increase the attendance at the meetings?' and "How am we retain our members ?"—ln the course of a thoroughly interesting discession which ensued, Bro. War- burton, W.C.T., said he thought one way to make their lodges more interesting would be to open them at proper time, get the business done, and then hold harmonious and enjoyable meetings at the close.—Bro. George Clarke said members ought to be taught thoroughly the Good Templar principles that intoxicating liqaors were bed in any form, that they were poisonous if taken in small quantities in being 1 injurious to the human system —Bro. Jameson maintained 1 that Good Tempter lodges should be A sort of college for educating and strengthening the members in temperance principles.—Bro. Mole impressed upon the meeting the im- portance of looking after the absentees from their lodges; and Bro. John Jackson thought they all ought to be more united and earnest in the work the had taken in hand.— After a few remarks from Bro. Pearce, Bro. Willis, of I Ashton' pointed out that the minds of many of the working classes were too mach taken up with horse-racing, betting, . and gambling, and such evils, and unless they could alter ' the tastes and dispositions of the people they must never hope to bring pTiale to be earnest members of the Order.— Bro. John Tayldl7 suggested that they should get all mem- hers to attend some place of worship, as he thought that would tend to strengthen them in their efforts—Bros. J. Barnard and J. Gee also spoke; the discussion thoroughout being an instructive one. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CAMP MEETING AT HAYDOCK.— The annual camp meeting in connection with the Primitive ' Methodist Society at Havdock was held on Sunday, and was con:leer:V-1 by Messrs. Thomas Clarke (Earlestown), Hanky I (Parr), J. Livesley (Ilaydock), and John Jackson (Earls-. I town). In the forenoon the friends miesioned the neigh- bourhood, and in the afternoon held a hearty and moderately well attended gathering on a plot of land adjoin- ing the chapel. A public love feast was held in the chapel in the evening. SERIOUS FIRE AT THE Vutc arr.— An alarming fire broke out in a dwelling-house in WI-wick-row, Vulcan, on Wed- nesday forenoon, and before the flames were extinguished considerable damage was done. The cottage in question is occupied by a party named Ellis, and while Mm. Ellis was at in the kitchen she heard a "crackling "noise upstairs. lOn giving an alarm and calling in a neighbour it was found that one of the bedrooms was on fire, information of the outbreak was sent to the Vulcan iron foundry, and several men from those works attended in order to suppress the flames. The fire rapidly spread in the meantime, and much excitement and alarm was manifested by the neighbours. Some of the burning materials were thrown out of the build- ing, while buckets of water extinguished others, and ultima- tely with some difficulty the fire was put out. The bed and bedding, two chairs, boxes, and other articles were entirely destroyed.

THE ANTI-VACCINATION AGITATION AT EARLES- TOWN.—PUBLIC MEETING. The fines and orders m tele upon 11 persons at a recent Petty Sessions held at Newton Town Hall created consider- able interest throughout the town. It is well known that a pretty strong feeling against compulsory vaccination exits among a large number of the inhabitants, and on Wednes- day evening a public meeting for the purpose of forming an "anti-vaccination insurance society" was held m the Co- operative Hall. Considering that the meeting had not been publicly announced, either by placard or circular, there was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. John Clarke, and there were also present Mr. Thornae Dusbury (of Blackburn), Mr. Joseph Emmett, Mr. B. Harrison, Mr. W. Gilmour, Mr. Latham, Mr. A. Forster, Mr. Wolfrnden, and others.—ln his opening remarks the Chairman said be regretted there were no ladies present, as it was a ladiee' question. He thought they must all be united upon the , question which had called them together, or it was certain they would fail. In any case they must have determina- tion. He maintained that the vaccination qzestion was the most important question of the day ; and they were desirous of giving their children from the so-called pure lymph, which was nothing better thin poison. which the doctors put into the blood of their children. If they only looked round their own neighbourhood they would find a few who had been injured very much by vaccina'ion, and he had no doubt there were many others of whom they did not know. It was important that they should take some steps upon the Matter and take a stand against vaccination, and then they would be on the right side. They might de- pend upon it that if they did so they would prove success- ful in the end. (Applause.)—Mr. Benjamin Harrison said he understood that the meeting was not to be one cf speeches, but to form an insurance society in relation to vaccination. He, however, thought it would be well to talk a little about the subj !ct in order that some persons present might gain information. Let them take the doctors' side of the question first. How did they prove that vaccination was a good thing? He had considered both sides of the ques- tion, and the main point of the doctors was that they proved everything by statistics. But he wanted to know where they got the statistics in the first place. They made it out that .vaccination was a good thing before there had been any vaccinator—(laughter)—they took a leap in the dark' He alluded to Dr. Jenner's work upon vaccination, sad how lymph was procured, and went on to say that in cases of death from smallpox, where It was stated in the statistics that the deceased persons had not been vaccinated, upon an examination and Inquiry being made it was found that they really bad been vaccinated. He thoughts there-

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 28, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 28, 1884.

fore, that that showed there was no reliance to be placed upon the statistics, and the doctors ought not to foist such statistics on the people as being true when they were false. (Hear, hear.) There was not a medical man in tne world who would say he could analyse lymph and say whether It was pure or not. The highest and best chemists they had could not find any difference between diseased lymph, and as they called it, lymph from a healthy child. What I reason bad they then to foist such a theory like that upon them? It seemed as if God sent children into the world and they were not pure or right unless they were marked or stamped with the mark of the beast. If a person would at- tend to physiological laws, and not have bad sanitary arrangements about them they were perfectly impervious to any disease. They were met that evening to form an insur- ance society to help parents who felt they had an objection to that beastly operation and yet could not afford to pay the fines. It would be what they called a self-help society— they would all help One another. They were met to discuss the rules. to say how it should be managed and who should manage it. He afterwards introduced Mr. Duxbury to the meeting, and spoke of the ability with which that gentleman had conducted cases at the police court, at Skipton and other places.—Mr. Thomas Daxbury, of Blackburn, re- ceived a rearm welcome. He remarked that if he could do anything at all to help them be should be quite willing to do so, but there was one dif- ficulty with him at present, and that was, how did they intend to proceed. He did not want them to think that the vaccination question was an easy question, or that the defence to their cases was at all easy. He did not wish them to think that there was any special qualifica- tion in him for the work, for if he was in any way superior to those present it was only by his experience in such cases. The law allowed a layman to appear when authorised by a defendant in any case under the Vaccinaticn Acts, and by that clause he had a legal right to represent any defendant who desired it. He would recommend each and everyone to make up their minds that their child should neither be butchered or vacccinated, for it was necessary that they should come to that conclusion firet. Having made up their minds to that effect, it was necessary that they should have some sort of an organisation to assist and support them. Any one might be broken down when standing alone' but by combination they had mutual theught and mutual understandings, and they could mutually help each other in various ways. After deciding not to vaccinate their chil- dren, which wag not only a beastly but a hellish process, they wanted to cell their friends and associates together and decide upon what their course should be. He suggested the appointment of a committee by that meeting to consi- der the rules of an insurance soci.ty, and proceeded to say that anti-vaccinators met with little sympathy from the magistrates. Whether or not a case was dismissed resh-d entirely with the ma?i-trites, whatever objections might be raise l or however illegal the proceedings hitherto I might have been. He all :cid to the s cietv in ex stance at Blackburn, and pirated out that the mcoe agitation they made and the more the question was brought before the public the greater was their success. He impressed upon them the necessity or organising themselves in self-defeece, for by so doing they would become stronger than if they acted as units Since compulsory vaccination came in vogue there Ilei been an increase of about four-fold in the deaths of children, notwithstanding the better food, the better sani- tary arraneements, and the better morality there was in the country. The question was one fully worth their while to consider. He knew of no question within the range of the House of Commons so great as that question; there was no question which extended wider or rested higher than that question It affected everyone of them, and not only them- selves, but their children. They had their blood so mixed with others by one adulterous union that they scarcely knew who they were, whether they were themselves or not, or in what proportion. (Laughter and applause.) If they sowed in the flesh corruption what could they expect? Could they expect anything diseased to promote health or happiness ; Could they expect a child that was tainted physically be have its mind morally pure? Did not the soul of man depend upon the state of the body in which it was located, and how could they therefore expect to have a pure thought and mind in an unhealthy body? (Applause.)—The Chairman stated that it was evident anti-vaccinators had to fight their case at a very great disadvantage. Their opponents made statements which were found to be neetrue. Vaccination was either right or wrong, and it ought to be conteaded on both aides in a fair and upright manner.—Mr. B. Harrison read over a set of rules for the suegested insurance society ; after which Mr. Gilmour said be hoped they would maintain their rights as ratepayers, and exercise the privilege they possessed in the election of members of the Board of Guardians with whom rested the power of ordering prosecu- tions. He had a right to defend his own child, and he in- tended to do it. He hoped they would press forward the insurance scheme, for if it worked well at Blackburn it would work well eleewhere.—The Chairman expressed the opinion that it was a questioe for everybody: not simply for the fathers and mothers, but the young men and young women of the present day.—Mr. Gilmour remarked that some persons might think they were pressing the insur- ance scheme because a few of them were likely to be fined on an early date, but he could inform them that those who were fined irtended to pay their flues themselves individually for the present. (Applause.) —After some farther discussion Mr. Sugden moved, and Mr. J. Muscroft seconded, that a society on the basis suggested be formed.—The motion was carried unanimously; after which the following committee was elected :—Messrs. Stag- den, W. Gilmour, Jolley, Gernett, B. Harrison, Stanley, Wolfenden, Latham, Higgins, J. Itlnscroft, J. Clarke, and A. Forster. Mr. A. Forster, of Regent-street, was appointed hon. secretary pro gene—On the Tradition of Mr. Gilmour, seconded by Mr. Harrison. a cordial vote of thanks was ac- corded to Mr. Daxbury for his address: and a similar com- pliment was paid to the chairman on the motion of Mr. B. Harrison. seconded by Mr. A. Forster—The meeting then concluded.

law of man, whilst there is another law incomparably more binding upon him, to which he makes no reference. This law is the jaw of God; and by the ligl t of this law, as laid down in the Gospel of Jesus Christ, I submit that he cannot justify this trafficking in holy ground and means of grace. But besides our duty towards God, the Christian religion embraces the performance of a duty towards someone else, viz., towards our neighbour, and here the golden rule " Whatever ye would that men should do unto you, even so do unto them " is applicable. If Canon Carr were a working-man what would he like to be dune? Would he wish to be able to enter his parish church feeling that it was his own, and that the same respect was paid to him there as to the richest man in the parish, or would he like to be subjected to arrangements which proclaimed him an interior? A poor man assuredly does not wish to have his p.,verty exposed to the woild, and hence he, the Vicar, must treat him as he would wish to be treated himself under like circumstances. Hence he must decide in favour of a free parish church in which alt his parishioners, rich and poor alike, will be placed on an equal footing. The words of the Archbishop of York, spoken some time ago at Shef- field, are applicable to St. Helens Church. They were— " That against which! do protest is that unhappy distinc- tion between the man who pays and he who does not pay when they come into the house of God The question is shall every man in this great town who lives by his industry be able to go to the church door, the door of his parish church, with the full conviction that it is his own, and that when he is there he is equal to all the rest who go to worship God there, and be treated there as their equal 2"
PROPOSED UNIVERSAL FEDERATION OF GLASSMAKERS.

For sometime past tnose interested in the manufacture of glass in England, America, and other countries have been discussing the advisability of forming one grand union or federation, comprising the whole of the glassworkers in the two hemispheres, and meetings upon the question have been I held at various glass-making centres. A meeting for the purpose of forming a branch in St. Helens—the leading glass-making centre in this country—was held in the Circus, St. Helens, on Sunday forenoon. There are already branches of the federation in Belgium, France, and America, and an effort is being made to include Eog,land in the amalgamation. During the preceding week a preliminary meeting of the window-glass makers of St. Helens was held, and it was resolved to join the federation. At last Sunday's meeting Mr. William Rigby, president of the local associa- tion, occupied the chair, and he was supported on the plat- form bydelegates from America, Belgium, Italy, and France, including Mr Isaac Cline, of America, president of the Universal Federation, and Andrew Bartt, s-cretary to the American Window-glass Workers' Association. The first speaker was Mr. Henry Burtt, of America, who read the following letter from Mr. H. Broadhurst, M.P., and Mr. T. Burt, M.P. :—" We wish to express the interest we feel in the present mission. We think it is very noble and public-spirited for the federation to send foreign dele- gates to England and other countries with the object of organising the working-mete connected with the glass trade. We are fully convinced that the best hope, if not the only hope, of the working people everywhere is in a thorough'and complete union. By combining they will not only improve their own condition, but they will also _make it easier for

those who are already organised, and will join their efforts to maintain any advantage they already posaess. We were very pleased to learn that the visits of delegates to France, Germany, and America were attended with such a large measure of success. We trust that a still greater measure of success will attend your meetings in Lancashire and other parts of the country."—Mr. Isaac Cline (of America), in the course of an able address, pointed out that since the forma- . . . . .

lion of the federation in Armerica and other countries there had been a very considerable increase in the remuneration for labour in the glass trade ; and he expressed a hope that the English glass trade by joining the federation would par- ticipate of the same benehts and place themselves beyond a position of pauperism. (Applause.)—Mr. Delawarrt, secre- tary of the Belgian Association (whose address was inter- preted by M. Ernest Stanzer); M. Barrt, president of the French Association, and M. Tailleur ; Mr. John Simcox, a delegate from Spon-lane, Birmingham ; Mr. Brown, from Sunderland ; Mr. Robert Hunter, secretary of the St. Helens Glass Bottle-makers' Aseociation •, and Mr. John Cross, agent of the St. Helens Miners' Pro- tection Association, also addressed the meeting. In the course of the proceedings the Chairman stated that not only were the wages lower in St. Helens than elsewhere but the men were bound down in one house in particular by having to sign a six months' engagement, so that no matter to what extent the price of glass increased their miserable pittance remained the same. (" Shame.")—Mr. French, delegate from Sunderland, said the glase cutters of Sunder- land were at present getting 259 a week, and to get that re- muneration they had had two strikes. For what, the em- ployers paid the men, 4s 6cl per day, they (the employers) received £2 63 3d, so that they had £9 13 3d profit per day out of each glasscutter. Now he contended that out of such profits employers could well afford to pay each man 10s per day. (Applause.) The Chairman asked if those present were in favour of the St. Helens Association joining the federation, and every hand was held up.—The various dele- gates then shook hands in celebration of the event.—A hearty vote of thanks to the foreign delegates concluded the proceedings.

COUNTY COURT.—WEDNESDAY. (Before T. P. E. Thompson, Esq ,judge) SINGULAR DISPUTED LOAN TRANSACTION.—Henry Atkin- son, of Lugsmore-lane, sub-contractor on the new County Asylum works at Rainhill, sought to recover £l2, money alleged to have been lent, from Thomas B. Patterson, clerk of the Asylum works, and residing at Eccleston Park—Toe plaintiff was represented by Mr. Malkin, and Mr. Smith ap- peared for the defendant —The plaintiff's case was that eirly in January. 18i3, defendant asked him for the loan of £l5, and he (plaintiff) agreed to lend him the amount by L 1 weekly instalments. On the 7.6 th January he lent defen- dant .£l, and he had let him have that amount weekly until it reached £l2. The defendant pro nised to pay him back when be got better off.—The defence was an emphatic denial of the statement that he bad borrowed the money. The de- fendant produced his works-book to show that on the 27th January, 17th February, and 24th March, days on which in- stalments were said to have been paid to him„ he was not at the works.—His Honour said there was too much doubt in the case to enable him to give a favourable verdict on the point, and all he could say was the plaintiff had not made out the case to his satisfaction. Between the two he was rather inclined in favour of the defendant if he was obliged to give a decision. The plaintiff might easily have pro- tected himself by getting defendant's initial, and he could hardly understand a man lending pound after pound for week after week and not getting the slightest acknowledg- ment. He would give judgment for the defendant, with costs.

AN "LOU." TRANSACTION.—Messrs. John Billings and Thomas Burrows sued Joseph Pilkington for the re- covery of £4 Bs, balance of a sum Gf money owing under an "LOU." for £lo.—Mr. Riley, who appeared for the plain- tiffs, stated that his clients were the executors of a late Mr. Henry Burrows, who had had possession of the " Star " Race Grounds, at Parr, and the defendant Pilkington wished to secure possession of the grounds. An agreement was consequently drawn up, whereby Pilkington took the grounds for the sum of £3O. He paid £2O on account and gave an "1 0.U." for the remaining £lO, which was to be ' redeemed a week later. When Mr. Billings saw the defen- dant and expected to receive the £lO, the sum of £5 12s was banded over, leaving the balance of £4 Bs, which was claimed.—Mr. Swift appeared for the defence, and main- tained that the 81.1111 of SA 83 was deducted from the £lO in payment of a quarter's rent which was due; and submitted cross receipts on the agreement to that effect.—His Honour gave a verdict for the defendant. DECEASED BROTHER'S ACCDUNT.—A grocer and pro- vision dealer at Huvton and ttainhill, named Reichardt, sought to recover £l5 158 41 from a single young woman named Kenny, formerly a beer-house keeper at Prescot, as administrattix of the estate of her brother, the late Mr. Kenny, teamsman.—Mr. Malkin appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. T. 0. Swift defended.—The sum named was the balance of an account owing for corn and other provender supplied to the late Mr. Kenney; and the defence was that all the brother's assets had gone towards the payment of his debts, while an amount of £8 receiven from his club bad gone towards the cost of the grave and funeral expenses.— Verdict for the defendant.

THE PEW QUESION AT THE PARISH CHURCH. No settlement has yet been corns to in rela:ion to the much-discussed question of abolishing the system of letting and assessing pews in the St. Helens Parish Church, thereby making it" free and open." It will be recollected that the late wardens (Major Windus and Mr. G. J. Critchlev), under the impression that the system was illegal, stated a case to Dr. Tristram) Q C., who gave an opinion upon it that the Church of St. Helens was originally a Chapel of Ease to the Prescot Church, and so remained until it was constituted the parish church f r the new parise of St. Helens by the Order in Council deted January 24th, 1853. It was clear ecclesiastical law that pews or sittings in a parish church or chapel of ease could not legally be sold or let except by the provisions of a special Act of Parliament or of the Church Building Acts, to which it had not been subject. The assessments, therefore, in counsel's opinion, could not be enforced, and might he treated as invalid without having recourse to any court to declare them invalid. The Rev. Chancellor Espin also stated that he had no doubt whatever that Dr. Tristram was right throughout. But the vicar (the Rev. Canon Carr, LL.D ), who has been in St. Helens for 38 years, holds other views on the subject, and has given expression to them in a pamphlet which he has recently published, with the title " Facts and Fallacies respecting the Parish Church of St. Helens, with some ac- count of its origin and constitution." The pamphlet is one of 10 pages, its price 2d, and according to a notice on the cover " The profits arising from the sale, if any, are to be added to the churchwardens' fund." In the course of the work the vicar states that so many misstatements have been lately circulated respecting the Parish Church of St. Helens that it seemed desirable to give a statement setting forth the leading facts of the church's history. The pamphlet continues :—" The grand and leading error that pervades all that has been said or written is the effort to prove that pew rents are unlawful in all parish Churches. This error arises from not distinguishing between ancient and modern parish churches. In ancient parish churches pew rents are unlaw- ful, because the churches having been built by a rate laid on the whole parish, the church is common property; whereas in hundreds of parish churches built under Acts of Parliament, a portion of the sittings, generally one-half, are rented. Of this St. Thom ts', Ecoleston ; St. Peter's, Parr ; Holy Trinity, Parr Mount; which are all parishes, are ex- amples. It is eherefore utterly beside the mark to argue that St. Helens Church must be free and open to all parishioners, because Prescot and Wigan and Warrington parish churches are free and open. If a little mere time and patience had been used, before rash statements had been put forth, it might have saved much unpleasant feeling and irritating remarks. Ills argued, however, that St. Helens is a Chapel of Ease to Prescot, and being such, is subject to the same laws as Prescot. And such it was stated to be in the case submitted to Dr. Trietram. On this statement depends the value of the opinion. If St. Helens Church Can be shame not ever to have been a Chapel of Ease to Prescot, the opinion is worthless.' Canon Car then proceeds to quote Roger& (in his Ecclesi- astical Law) as to what constitutes a legal ch tpel of ease, and argues that these conditions are not fulfilled in St. Helen's church ; neither was it an ancient church; and hence the law affecting the legality of pew rents in those cases could have no obligation to St. Helens, Continuing., Canon Carr says:—" What specially marks St. Helens to have been a proprietaey chapel is the repairs, not a paro- chial matter, but are to be done out of the funds of the chapel itself.' hut it is argued, that by order of the Queen in Council, St. Helens was created a parish, and the church thereby having been made a parish church, it became un- lawful to let pews. The answer is that so far from forbid- ding the letting, the order practicallY recognises both the letting and selling of pews; otherwise the words 'owner ' and 'occupier' which frequently occur in it have no mean- ing. Secondly, there are hundreds of parish churches in which pews are let, and legally so. The error lies in sup- posing that the order iite council placed St. Helens on the same footing as an ancient parish church. But, traffic in church property, it is said, is odious.' Then ge;, rid of it. But, as regards the free and open system, there is, practically 'more of sentiment than of reality in it. In all so called free and open churches, the appropriation of seats is at the bishop's disposal, and subject to him, at the djaposal of the churchwardens. And, as a rule, notably in our own neighbourhood, as elsewhere, the poor avoid enter- ing the seats usually occupied by the well-to-do of the con- gregatien in churches free and open. The plan now adopted, at the Bishop's suggestion, in our own church, removes every reasonable objection; and insets every real want, by making every sitting available. It secures to the regular occupiers their places, and mikes any unoccupied room availaele for corners after the service has commenced. The church at present contains-about 250 pews, hold as fellows: —65 pews owned by 42 members of the congregation; 54 pews owned by 25 nen-members of the congregation; 42 pews owned by the curate fund and let; 44;pews owned by the cnrate fund but allet, these are mostly in the galleries; pews behind the organ, and therefore useless; 36 pews free. The total free accommodation is about 250 sittings. The payments made in respect of these pews are approxi- mately :—.6144 to the curate fund; and,.£l4B to private owners. It must be borne in mind that this sum of £l4B represents approximately the whole sum payable to private owners, if all the pews were let, but mtny of these, especi- ally in the gallery, are indet, and the amount actually paid cannot be estimated as exceeding £l2B, at the outside. From this again must be deducted the assessment on the 74 pews, which has to be ?aid to the curate fund, amounting to about £O, thus reducing the actual net amount received by the pew owners to less than £lOO a yeareinstead of £3OO as has been stated. The church or curate fund receives about £l4O, which would otherwise have to lre raised by collections or subscriptions. The agitation referred to has for its object, as I understand, the making of the whole ac- comodation in the c'eurch absolutely free; and with regard to this we must consider whether such a change would be for the benefit of the church and the comfort of the congre- gation. On this point opinion is divided t In many churches where it has been adopted, notably in Liverpool, it has been declared a failure. In the churches referred to the congre- gations have not been increased by the change, the amount of the offertory has not been found sufficient to replace the the amount formerly received from pew rents, and the [Wm- hers of the congregation have lost more in comfort than they have gained in money." In concluding, Canon Carr states: —" rn what has been stated, it has been shown, as I think, Ist. That Dr. Tristram's opinion is woitaless, having been based on a defective case; 2nd. That pew rents are legal in all, except in ancient Parish churches; 3rd. That pew rents and assessments in our own church having been established by those who built the church at their own.cost and hav- ing continued for 289 years, are legally and morally bind- ing, except on the poor, for whom provisioa is made; 4th. That the amount paid to private owners has been greatly overstated; sth. That the mixed system, partly free and partly rented, is, as a rule, the best and most convenient (thei "free and open being, in many cases, expedient or neces sary), and that it is placed beyond objection, where all un- occupied sittirms are made open after the service commefices. 6th. That St. Helens and the surrounding districts are not in a state of the great spiritual destitution which has been asserted. As to the aspersions cast upon myself, my only reply is, my manner of life for 38 years in St. Helens. I venture to hope that the exolanation thus given, will satisfy all reasonable and unprejii lined minds, and may re- move erroneous impressions from those who may have honestly taken up views not justified by facts." t A correspondent signing himself " C.E.L." writes as fol- lows:—The Vicar of St. Helene has been endeavouring, by the publication of a piper, entitled " Facts and Fallacies." to prove that pew ren.s in his parish church are "legal." In using the term legal, it is understood that,he is referring to the
