LOWTON PARMR CitußCEr TR& PARTY.—Oh Friday, the annual tea parry was held in the boys' school in connection with Lowton Parish Chursh. The scholars assembled at two o'clock, and headed by the Lowton Brass Band, the rector, the Rev. R Smith, and the churchwardens, Messrs. Peak, rayter, and Laycock, walked through the principal lanes of the parish. The procession was a large one, and had a gay appearance. In front of the band was carried the new silk banner recently purchased, which was much admired. At Lowton House, the residence of Robert Houghton, E. 4 , JP., the band and teachers received refresh- ments, and Mr. and Miss Houghton presented every scholar and teacher, numbering 240, with an orange and some gin zerbread. The procession then marched to Lyme House, the residence of W. H. Arnett, Erg., where they were again provided with refreshments, and all the scholars and teachers received at the hands of Mrs. Arnett a neatly decorated card bearing a teat of Scripture. From this place they pro- ceeded by Lane Head to the schools, when about 400 scholars and friends sat down to tea. The party afterwards adjourned.. to the cricket field, where a variety of gam.e, dancing, &el, were engaged in. Votes of thanks were given to the ladies who presided at the tea trays, to the sub- scribers to the tea party fund, the rector, and teachers, and a very pleasant evening was brought to a close soon after i ten o'clock.

HOLIDAY FESTIVITTES r GOLBORNE.—Last week, when I the annual races at Newton Common took place, was gener- ally observed as a holiday, the various mills and workshops i closing on Thursday morning. The annual school gatherings were held on the Friday, particulars of which are appended : —St. Thomas's CAurch : The scholars, teachers, and friends met at one o'clock, and conducted by the rector, the Rev. C. T. Quirk, M.A., and the Rev. W. Thorp, MA., curate, a procession was formed and flags and banners dis- tributed to the scholars. Headed by the Golborne Brass Bind (conductor, Mr. P. Cook). the procession moved off to Golborne Smithies, and from thence down Church-street, High-street via Parh View, to the residence of Mt. Brewis, 1 who regaled the numerous company with oranges, the ; band playing a pleasing selection of music during the , visit. The processienists then returned to the schools, where tea was provided, upwards of 700' sitting down. The evening was spent in the cricket field, the band playing for dancing until dusk.— AU Saints' C.ztheic. School : A large congregation assem- bled in the chapel abut two o'clock. Headed by the Edge Green brass band (conductor, Mr. T. Hibbert), a procession marched towards Golborne Smithies, returning through Park-view. Born-lane, down Legh-street, and on to the school. The new silk banner bearing the words" All Saints,. Golborne," we much admired. lietween 600 and 700 sat down to tea. M. John Haworth' field was again set apart for recreation in the evening, and a most enjoyable time was spent. Father Byrne was indefatigable in his efforts to• make the proceedings a success —Congregationalists : The Congregationalists mustered at the chapel, and a procession was formed. A halt was made opposite the residence of Mr. Yates, where one of Sankey's songs:was sung, as also at the residences of Mrs. Travers, Mr. W. Mitchell, and Mr. Davies. At the two last mentioned refreshment in the shape I of oranges was provided. On returning to the school I about 250 partook 'of tea. The usual out-door amusements ' were resorted to in the evening, Mr. Birchall's field providing ample accommodation.— Indepenicnt Methodists: The scholars, teachers, and friends met at the school, and in processional order paraded the streets, halting at several points to sing. The Manches:er Whit-week collection of hymns was used. About 180 sat down to tea in the schoolroom. In a field lent by Mr. Pierpnint amusements were continued until nine o'clock,— Primitive .3fethodists : The Primitive Methodists con- nected with Golborne, Edge Green, and Lowton-road schools met at the Smithies early in the afternoon, and pro- ceeded along some of the streets. The scholars of the re- spective schools afterwards proceeded to their respective headquarters. where tea was served. The Edge Green scholars in the evening occupied a field in the Wigan-road, lent by Mr. Lowe; the Golborne contingent had their usual field belonging to Mr. John Bate and the Lowton- . road friends adj urned tons field adj went to their premises. ; Wesleyan Methodists: The Wesleyans had a cheap ex- cursion to Southport for the day. The party left Golborne by the ordinary 6.31 a.m. train, and returned by the- 7-45 • n.m. from Southport, special carriages being provided. The B aptist schools, situated near the station at Southport, ; were again engaged, and here breakfast and tea was pro- . vided. The day being beautifully fine the out was thoroughly enjoyed.

DEATH OF Ma. RAwmrrs.—After a very brief but pain- ful illness the death of Mr. Charles Edward Rawlins, senior , partner in the firm of Rawlins and Son, Brook Works, Lea Green, took place on Thursday week at his residence, Rock I Mount, Rainhill, in his 73rd year. The deceased, who was a firm and consistent Liberal politician, was in his younger days an active member of the Anti-Corn Law League. The funeral took place on Monday. The cortege left the resi- dence of the deceased gentleman on Raiahill Mount, and proceeded to Sraithdown-lane Cemetery, where the inter- ment took place. The service at the house and also at the grave side was conducted by the Rev A Armstrong, minis- ter of Hope-street Unitarian Chapel. Besides the family of the deceased there were present the Rev J Barton, vicar of Rainhill, Mr E C Poore, Mr T Harmer, Mr A Cross, and many of the leaders in the Liverpool Liberal party ; and all the employee of the firm of Messrs G E Rawlins and San. The deceased gentleman has taken a most active part in, the diffusion of the principles of Liberalism, both in Liver- pool and South-West Lancashire. He has always identified himself with the cause of progress, social, educational, and , political. Assisted by the late Mr James Harvey and other prominent Liberals of Liverpool, he became one of the pro- moters and chief supporters of the "Mechanics Institution,' the first School of Art in Liverpool, and the Brougham Institute," whose function was the spread of Liberalism by means of free lectures and the institution of newsrooms and readingrooms for the working classes. Daring the great Reform contest he threw the whole of his energies into the Anti-corn Law struggle, assisting in the formation of the Liverpool branch of the Anti-corn Law League, but finding, with other young politicians, that the principles of the league were not sufficiently advanced, he inaugurated the "Anti Monopoly Association," which aimed at total repeal, and as hon. sec. contributed greatly to its success. From 1858 Mr. Rawlins was a dilector of the Itlxchange Building Company, and member of the Liverpool Chamber of Com- merce, of which he was president in 1867. He took a strong personal interest in the Hungarian struggle, and entertained Louis Kossuth at his house in Prince's Park during that patriot's visit to Liverpool. In scholastic matters, he was a warm supporter of the nndenominationa/ school system, building'and establishing at his works at Mickleheact Green the first undenonsinationd school in South Lancashire. To his workmen he was always a kind master, building for them healthy homes, educating their children, and provi- ding gymnastic appliances and other entertainments for their amusement. Ey all acquainted with,him, he will sin- cerely regretted as a warns friend, a kind master, and a steadfast adherent to•the cause of progress.-

div.p: The Conservatives prudently resolved not to contest the seat for Leicester, and Mr. J. A. Picion, was on Thursday elected without opposition. Mauctons Acr.—Two men named Gilder, father and son, were brought up for sentence on Wednesday, at the Livarpool Sessions, having been found guilty of maliciously destroying a quantity of yeast, the property of Messrs. Caine and Galbraith, bakers. The prisoners were dealers in yeast, and, with the view of injuring the prosecutors' busi- ness, contrived to mix carbolic acid and ammonia with some of their yeast, which was lying at the railway station. The Recorder said the offence was most wicked and malicious. Be sentenced the elder prisoner to six menthe and the son to three months' imprisonment. PRESENTATIONS. TO A CONGREGATIONAL MINISTER.--OE Saturday afternoon the scholars of the Peasley Cross Con- gregational Sunday School were regaled with their annual treat in specially fine weather. About 500 scholars, teachers, parents, and friends gathered at the school and proceeded to the picturesque grounds of Mr. Richard Pilkington, Rainford Hall. The usual games and amusements were heartily entered into, and a capital tea was partaken of. Is hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Pilkingtoa for his kindness in allowing the use of his grounds, and three cheers for Ms. Pilkington were also given. At the oall of Mr. Wm. Smith three cheers were given for the Rev. C. H. Bradbury and Mrs. Bradbury. who made their first appear- ance after their wedding tour. Mr. Smith then presented Mr. Bradbury with a purse containing £4l 14s, as a mark of the respect and esteem of the congregation. He expressed the hope that Mr. and Mrs. Bradbury would be long spared, and that Mr. Bradbury's work would prosper. Mr. Gil- christ, on behalf of the Young Men's Christian Association, next presented to Mr. Bradbury a handsome timepiece (value £0); and Mr. J. H. Garner, secretary of the school, presented a handsome electro-plated biscuit-box on behalf of the Young Women's Class—The Rev. C. H. Bradbury duly responded, remarking that he was thankful his work solar had been appreciated, and be hoped now that he had brought a partner te help him his usefalness might be doubled.—Those present afterwards enjoyed themselves un- til dusk. AN ExPLANATtriL—It hat been said that OamstaGir & Co. are too pushing, and want to force their Mineral Waters down people's throats. Now this is putting it rather too strongly. They certainty want to get their Mineral Waters down people's throats, and why Because, if people's throats are to have Mineral Waters down them. Calitsucit'S ARE THE BEST for the eurpose. It is no credit to CAMMACK SCO to say that their Mineral Waters are the best in this neighbourhood, for they ought to be so, seeing that they are not manufactured by the old fashioned rue o' thumb methodi, but on the latest scien- tific principles, under the supervision of Mr. J. Cammack, Hence while first-class beverages are to be bought at low olass prices, Cammack tc Co. think it their duty to let the public know it. That Is why they unceasingly cry out "ALWAYS ACE FOB CAMM6.OO."—Advt,

RUNOORN AND WIDNES. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, Mr. W. Handley in the chair. Present : Messrs. T. Norman, Aaron, Midwood, Warburton, Darby- shire, J. Weir, Mclntire, Wallington, Hamilton, H. Limiter (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).—An account of £2l 18s 10d, re-payment of interest and loan for the hos- pital extension was passed. A letter was read from the Chief-Constable of Cheshire intimating that he should have no objection to Inspector Atherton being appointed assistant relieving officer for Runcorn, and the Chairman gave notice that he would move his appointment at the next meeting.—On the 13th June, Mr. W. J. Dansev, Local Government Board Inspector visited the house and reported that he found the wards and premises in a cleanly condition. Some of the yards needed repair, but he understood this ha.l generally been done by the inrn ites.—The Master (Mr. It Jones) reported that there were 172 inmates in the house as compared with 172 in the corresponding week last year. During the week 12 vagrants ' had been relieved. There were 15 imbeciles or idiots in the house and 36 lunatics in the asylum. Twenty-eight boys and 27 girls were in attendance at school, and 4 boys and 15 girls were receiving industrial training. During the week 379 persons had been relieved in Runcorn at a cost of £37 144 6d, 148 persons at Frodsham at a cost of £l5 6s, and 129 persons at Badworth at a cost of £l4 2a 61.

div.head: WIDNES ATHLETIC CLUB SPORTS.
div.p: WIDNES ATHLETIC CLUB SPORTS.

The seventeenth annual festival in connection with the Widnes Athletic Club, which was commenced on Friday evening, was continued on Saturday. . Tbe weather was beautifully fine, and upwards of 5,000 persons assembled upon the ground. A considerable number of local gentry occupied seats on the grand stand. As usual the spurts were held under the laws of the Amateur Athletic Association, and were conducted in a manner which reflected the highest credit upon the officials, whose names are as follow, : Judges: Messrs E Bolton, E A Chorlton, T T Matthieson, aril A McClellan (white) ; clerks of the course, Messrs C Barlow, I Carr, D Forster, W B Longton, and D Matthieson (cerise); handicapper, official timekeeper, and referee, Mr Walter Platt (orange and black); starter, Mr Rat Cameron, junior, president West-lane Bicycle Club, and Liverpool Harriers (crimson); hon treasurer, Mr James Hurst; • lion secretary, Mr C E Barlow; secretary, Mr Jones W Davies (dark blue). With a programme comorising 30 events, strict adherence to the times fixed is highly desirable and indeed necessary, if the proceedings are to work smoothly and give satisfaction to the spectators, and in this respect on Satur- day not the slightest fault could be found. Punctually at two o'clock, the first race, the 120 yards han- dicap, was commenced, and the starters out of 4S entries being (lithe up to the average, some fine running was witnessed, the " time " eing very good. Less interest than nseal was manifested in the long distance races in consequence of the absence of George and Snooks, who were opposing each other at a more important meeting. but the struggle for supremacy in each instance was very spirited. The bicycle contests were very keenly disputed, and the ground being very hard, the speed all round was very creditable. One or two spills " took place, but happily without serious results to the riders. The local competitors were very unfortunate in all the events, by far the greatest proportion of the first prizes going to the neigh- bouring city of Liverpool. The most interesting feature of the afternoon was the gymnastic display of a company of athletes from the Liverpool Gymnasium, under the direc- tion of the talented Mr. A. Alexander, and that the specta- tors were delighted with the skilful and graceful way in which the performance was gone through was testified to by the frequent and hearty applause accorded to this athletes. The company included Meows. R S Thomas, G Hushforth, E Taylor, R Brunton, J G Crook, J Singleton, R Cave. 11 Houghton, E Alexander, S Rose, It W Allmev, G W Bar- ker, and A B Crawford. We ought to mention that during the afternoon the Star of Temperance Braes Band, under the leadership of Mr. Wm. Jennett, played an admirable selection of music. The results of the various events were as follows :

BOATING FATALITt NEAR CARDIFF: FOUR.' LIVES LCST. —On Wednesday. afternoon a pleasure boat left Penarth for a sail, containing, it was said, eight persons. A tug boat passing the party, an attempt was made by the boeman to hook on to the tug, and the pleasure boat at once capsized. A passing pilot boat picked up some of the party, hurt three adults and two children were drmned. A later telegram says :—" One child, not two, was drowned. The names of the three adults who lost their lives were Harriet Baker, married ; Annie Burton, of Newcastle, married ; and John Boyle, of Penarth."

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workouse, Warrington, on Wednesday morning. There were present—Messrs Greening (in the chair), Darbyshire. TENDER Fon Criss—The House Committee recom- mended that the tender of Mr. Speakman for growing grass, a 101, be accepted.—Mr. BLLcuirrasr thought they had made a very good bargain.—On the motion of the CHAIR" MAN, the recommendation was adopted. THE PLACING our OF CHILI/SEN.—The School Commit- tee recommended that in future none of the boys and girl° should be hired out of the Warrington Union unless under exceptional circumstances.—Mr. DARSYSHIRF moved the confirmation of these minutes, and explained that what Nr4s meant by "exceptional circumstances" was cases of chil- dren being placed-out with relatives and such like. The/ had had a good deal of difEcialty with children who were sent out of the Union, whilst at the same time they lu! plenty of applicitions for children from persons living ,12 the Uction.—Mr. BLACKHIIRJE seconded the proposal, whice lettet

The audit stated that it had transpired that during the half-year Mt audit some of the children had been absent frcan the Wor". house for a considerable period, and that the master con' sidered he was justified only in paying for the maintenance., of the children for the number of weeks they were actualll in the Workhouse. How many sticks go to the building of a crow's nest ? Nora, because all are carried. Why is the tongue of a busybody like an obstructionist M.P. ?—Because it is an unruly member. The man who prides himself on always speaking his mind is the first one to kick when he finds anybody else exercising the same privilege. ODD, WASN'T IT—Father—"l never imagined that your studies cost me so much money." Student—" Yes, and I don't study much, either." THEORY AND PRACTICE.—A man who lectured on" How to Win Success," a few nights ago, was trying to borrow 5 dollars an hour later to pay his fare out of town and liqui- date his hotel bill. He must have drawn a blank. The best and quickest way to revive a lady when she faints, is to begin taking down he hair. If it ain't her own she will grab it in a jiffy. A bachelor editor gives this as his prescription, and says the remedy is a certain cure. A CHILD NOT WANTING IN OBSERVATION.—A School. board inspector asked the members of a girls' sewing-class the other day, "Who can tell me what basting a turkey means ? " There was silence for a while, and then a little miss signified that she knew. "Well, what is it?" said the inspector. "Sewing up the place where the stuffin' goes in," was the reply. On a certain occasion at Indore, in Central India, n triumphal arch was put up. On one side were the words, "The Governor ,is coming," on the other side, "Heaven help us!" while at a certain station in the Berars, over the entrance of a cemetery, an arch was erected, on which was emblazoned for the edification of the expected magnate —" Welcome ! " Ma& MULBERRY'S CAKE.—" Wake up ! " exclaimed Mrs. Mulberry in aloud whisper, as she bunched the slumbering Mulberry in the short ribs t'ilth her elbow the other night; wake up! I'm sure I hear burglars down in the dining- room." "Don't disturb them, then," said the drowsy Mul- berry, turning over on the other side. "Bs just as quiet as you can, and maybe they will eat some of that fruit cake you have in the pantry." TOOK THE BAIT.—" Well, dear,4 temarked Mn. Smith, as her husband started emt for a day's fishing, "I hope you will be successful and 'arine. home a nice b sleet of trout." "Never fear," re3pon decl Smith "if teere are are any trout to be caught lam *le boy to catch 'em. It's a cold day in the spring time eehen a trout gets away from ins." "It is indeed," his -wire said; and, by the way, here is your Pocket-hr!e lying on the table. You mustn't forget thee. You ca'lit catch trout without bait, you know." 9.:ON'T LIKE THE SEGGESTION.—" My dear," remarked re Central-avenue young man to his best girl: "I see by the papers that a girl in Baltimore hat reduced the size of her month considerably by whistling." "That is singular, isn't it, George ?" replied the girl. "Yes, and it is said that after a few months praetice a four-inch mouth could be reduced to two inches and a half." "0 my, how queer." "Yes, dear, and I thought it would improve your looks if you were to try it." "You horrid thing! I'll never speak to you again—so there!" And that engagement is post- Poned. WHY HE lIIIDN'T.—" Did you notice what a boor that Man was who sat next to you ?" asked one lady of another as the pair stepped off a Woodward Avenue car the other day. "How ?" "Why he refused to pass up the fare for the lady ha lavender silk." "Oh, well, yon see they were divorced only two weeks ago, and it couldn't be expected that he would recover his composure thus soon. It is a mean trick in any divorced woman to expect her ex-husband to pass - alimony money up to the fare-box." HADN'T FAR TO DROP.—" Women," said old Mr. Squaggs, looking up front his paper, and placidly smoothing the shining surface of his bald head," women is strange creeturs They're different from men. It's a'most impossible to re- form 'em once they gets down. When a man falls from grace he soon gets up ag'in, but when a woman falls it sorter stems her like, and she don't have no ambition to rise ag'in. Yes, women is strange creeturs." "Yes," said old Mrs. Squaggs, thoughtfully, as she interrupted her knitting for a moment, "a man rises easily after he falls from grace, but you see he hain't fur to fall. With a woman it is different." WHY HE WENT TO THE CIRCUS. —There was a circus in the city the other day and old man Primus, who had braved the blasts of seventy winters, took a front seat at the perfor- mance. A yonng acquaintance, who came in and took a seat beside the old man, exclaimed :—" Way, Mr. Primus! I am surprised to see as old a man as you at a circus perfor- mance." "I always come," said the old man quietly. "I care nothing for the general performance, but I come to hear the clowns." "So you come to laugh at the jokes?" "Oh, no! I don't laugh at them any more!" replied the septua- genarian, "but I enjoy the jokes because they revive old memories, and take me back to my cnildhood days when I used to sit on my grandfather's knees and hear him tell them as they were told by the clowns when he was a boy." A Leven& OF THE AerriceerE.—Mrs. Limoges is very brie- a-brac in her tastes, but is not very ready to pay her bills. The other day the grocerymen "Can [see Mrs. L ?" he said to the servant, "What do you want?" "I've got a bill here for some groceries she bought last month." "Only ' a month old?" asked the girl, in surprise. "Ain't that old enough?" "No, sir; it is not. Mrs Limoges, I'd have you knew, is a lover of the antique, and should she see a hill only a month old she would haveea fit of nervous prostration" Well, that beats the deuce. When shall I come?" Oh, some time in the future. The older the bill gets the better; but clop% you ever dare to come around with any of those ,• vulgar new bills, that the stains of timehave never touched," and she slammed the door in his face. THE LAST ONE ON THE SACRED ELEPHANT.—TWO young ladies were gazing at the white elephant as it stood enthroned in all its sacred splendour, aod surrounded by the mystic em- blew of its holy character and the adoring priests who were kneeine• devoutly 03 every side. "Use curious it is," re- marked one. "that any race of people should be so deluded ' as to worship an elephant." "It is indeed," replied the other sadly. "When I look upon the worship deg throng of ig- norant, superstitious creatures and re .liee how earnest and sincere they are, I cannot but feel that there should be no rest until the missionary message is berne to the last one of these benighted heathen." "True,', asserted the first speaker," it is a grand and solemn duty—" Just at this juncture the animal flicked its tail and struck one of the Buddhist priests in the mouth. " Howlv Moses! " he ex- claimed, interrupting his devotions, "ye hethen baste" and then the young ladies strolled on to the moukey's cage. stx TIMES AN ORPHAN.—" You see," said the boy between his sobs, "we were all Mormons living down in Southern Utah, where dad was a bishop, and, of course, had five wives. Well, each one of them had a boy baby about the same age, and they were all named Brigham —." "lent it strange to name them all alike?" "rhey always name the first one Brigham, if it is a boy, and," said he," when we were about four years old dad used to drive the little flock of Brigiiams down to the farm and make us weed carrots. The farm was two miles from town, and one day when we were all alone a band of Indians kidnapped the whole of us and took us away down into Arizona. The other boys got sick and all died, but they kept me with them five years before I could escape, which I finally did, and got lick home Well, when I got -back I didn't know my mother or even her number, a,.d she didn't know me and they all claimed me as their little lost Brigham. So they had to draw cuts to Lee which one would have me; , and I was h r's till she died -then the next, and Bo on. My first mother died is year after I got home; then I became the son of mother nu tibtr two. She atioataVzed, ran away, and married a gentile, and got killed in a railrotd collision. I liked with this mother a year and a half. The third mother got hooked by to cow six mon hs after she had me. The fourth one died after I was 13, and my last mother died six months ago. An I no d id's dead. I tell you What's the matter, mister, Cliv don't know what real sorrow is till they've been an orphan like me, six times."

On arriving, Smiler found that his wife had retired to rest, knowing that her liege lord could let himself in by means of his latch key. Going into the kitchen in quest of something to eat, by way of supper, he found, to his delight, a slice of bread nicely covered with preserve. The pepper box stood in close proxi- mity to the bread, and Smiler accidentally knocked it over, but the match he had struck having gone out, he failed to notice whether or not the contents had touched his tit-bit. He had nearly "sided off" his "preserve butty," when the voice of his wife was heard, calling from the head of the stairs, "Smiler, mind theau doesnd touch that bread a' preserve at's o' th' end o' th' table, because it's getten pl.l/son on it." Smiler no sooner heard this admonition than, experiencing a smarting sensation in his mouth and stomach, he yelled oat— "Oh, Lord! Betty, aw'm peysoned, aw am for sure! Aw've etten enoof for t' kill ten men,—oh, dear !" and, ima- gination beginning to work upon Smiler, he writhed about in all the fancied symptoms of poisoning. " Betty ! Betty !' he gasped," come deawn at onst if I theaw wants t' see me alive. Th' peyson's gone i' mi legs awready, aw'm sure it has, an' if ha gets any fur aw'st be done for aw egether. Oh! Lord, ha' mercy on me, an' forgi' me my sins! Aw'm punish't neaw for neglectin' my wife an' childer, un all ut aw con do is t' make a will, leeavin' sawn Betty all 'at aveve getten t' leeav',—an' my debts t' pay !" By this time Betty was at her husband's side, and having heard that mustard and water were good to use in cases like Smiler's, she rushed into the back kitchen to procure the mustard. Deeming that by this time the poison must have get well into his system, she hastily made up her mind not to weaken the strength of the mustard by dilution; so, emptying a respectable quantity into her hand, and bidding Smiler to "shut his een an' oppen his meawth," she deftly deposited the condiment into the gaping orifice last men- tioned. Springing up from his position on the floor, he jumped about the room like one gone suddenly mad, his eyes fairly starting from their sockets with the pain he was at that moment suffering. "Host to feel any betther neaw, Smiler ?" was the anxious query of his wife, as she sat mutely watching Smiler's imita- tion of an Indian war-dance. " Betther ! betther l" he yelled, "aw feel as if ten theaw- sand feyres wur brunnin' my inside eawt—aw do! Oh, dear! oh, my !" he groaned, rubbing his chest, and rolling about in a paroxysm of pain and anguish, "aw never thowt aw ehould ha' deed eaut o' my bed o this'ns peysened; my wife al be a widow an' my childer faytherless 1 Lord, ha' mercy on my sinful sowl!" "Smiler," said Betty, tearfully, " dote think a sops o' whisky an' wayther ud do thee any good ?" "It met do,' was the ready response of Smiler. "But dunnot make it too wake or it'll ha' no effect uppo' my system in it present state. Oh, Betty !" he exclaimed, as another spasm of pain seized him, "aw feel aw'm goin' ! Come an' put thy arms reawnd my neck an' tell me 'at theaw forgies me for spendin' my time away fro thee an' not keepin' thee company awhoam !" Meanwhile Betty had gone to a cupboard for the little drop she kept for emergencies. Looking about she suddenly espied the identical bon-bouche upon which she had placed the poison intended for the delectation of the mice. Rushing to where poor Smiler lay groaning she joyfully exclaimed— " Why, Smiler, theavdt noan peysant afther aw! Here's what aw laid for th' meyce •, that 'at thou eat must ha' bin what eawr Tom loft afore he went t' bed. ANY see °ether thee or somelidy else has knookt th' pepper duster o'er, an' happen thatalacceawnt for th' smartin' i' thy meawth afore am gan thee thy mustard." To say that Smiler shed tears of joy when he feund one the mistake he had made, would convery a very inadequate idea of the thankfulness that had filled his heart. He wept, he prayed, and after throwing his arms around Betty's neck and promising to be a better husband in the future than he had been in the past, he, first fortifying his inner man with a basin of gruel, not to mention the addition of a good strong dose of whisky, went to bed a far happier man than he had been a short time previouely.—From Ben Brierley Journal.

SERIOUS CASE OF STABBING. As reported in our last issue, a man named James John- son, who lives in lodgings in Winwick-road, on Friday evening stabbed another Min who live: inthe same neigh- bourhood on the left shoulder, with a eLoe- maker's knife, doing him such injury as to neces- sitate removal to the Infirmary. Information was given to the police,`who took Johnson into custody. When apprehended he was bleeding very much from the nose, and a large mob of people had assembled round the house and were threatening io take the taw into their own hands. —Prisoner was on Saturday brought up at the Police Court, but as that portion of Winwick-road where he resides is in the county jurisdiction, he was handed over to the county police.—On Monday morning he was brought before Mr. Ziba Armitage, at the Occasional Court held at Mr. White's offices, when he was charged with unlawfully and mali- ciously wounding William Hall with a knife, on the 20th June.—The prosecutor, a toolmaker, of 271, Winwick-road, said that he was standing in the street near his house door at about six o'clock on Friday evening, when he heard a dis- turbance which appeared to be at the back of the house where the prisoner lodged, in the same street. He went to the yard dour of the house whence the noise of the disturb- ance proceeded, and saw the prisoner in the yard beating a woman. Witness and a man named Knott went into the yard, and prisoner went into his house, returning in about a minute with a shoemaker's knife in his hand. Witness then left the yard and had got a short distance away, when he felt a blow on the back of his left shoulder. He called out, "Am I stabbed?" and a man named Strkw said "You are." Prisoner went into the house, add rit.nets fointed from loss of blood add isot token WO fi neighbour's home. He was afterwards faked fp the Infirmary. ,He had never spoken to the prlsoner.—By the prisoner: You were beating your landlady. I did not see anyone beating you.—James Ellison, labourer, Winwick-road, spoke to seeing the prisoner go into his house, return with a knife, and strike Hall with it on the shoulder. Witness went to Hall's assistance, removed his clothing, and found` a wound on, the shoulder, which was bleeding very much. Prisoner appeared excited, ,and as though he had bad some beer. Did not hear Hall say anything to prisoner, or pri- soner say anything to Hall when he struck him.—By the prisoner: I did not see anyone beating ,you in the yard ; you were bleeding on the face.—William Straw, striker, r 6, Antrobus-street, Orford, also deposed to witnessing the attack, and further said that he afterwards sac the prisoner stiike at another man.—Dr. Richmond, house surgeon at the Warrington Infirmary, said that the prosecutor was admitted on Friday evening suffering from an incised wound about thretquarters of an inch long, on the left shoulder, and going down into the muscles of the back. He did not probe the wound, but it was not very deep. Hall had lost a con- siderable quantity of blood. Any sharp pointed .knife would have caused the wound. Prosecutor was doing well land was in no Whittiegbacn, who received the prisoner from the custody of the Boroueh Police, deposed that he stated the charge to the prisoner, who replied, "If I did I che not remember; I do not remember anything." Witness had searched for the knife, but it had not been found.—Prienner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial, being offered the opportunity of bail in two sureties of £2O each and himself in vq.

the probebility of a reduction of them. Thus, he thohlaht, the scheme was commended to their hearts approval and it was on these grounds that he supported the reeolutien. (Applause). Mr. W. Dinatc, who was seated on the platform, then rose to address the meeting, and was greeted with laughter ' and cries of "order," "sit down," and "turn him out," to which he responded "what are yen afraid of 2' Quietness having been restored the MAYOS said that if anyone desired to address the meeting and their observa- tions were of a relevant character he did not see how he could with any sense of justice refuse to allow them. (Ape plause.) Therefore he was bound to say that ste long as Mr. Diggle adhered' to die question before the meeting, and his arguments were of a relevent character and he did not wander from the subitet—(laughter)—he'vras quite in order in asking permission to address the meeting. Mr. UrGGLE, amidst ironical cheers, proceeded to say that he was a ratepayer and, property owner and that he thought that he had expended and laid out as much in Warrington in the shape of cottage property, as any a them, and per- haps more than some, when he was again interrupted. The MANOR: Mr. Diggle, I presume you are going to speak to the meeting? Mr. DIOGDR : I am. (Cries of "Go on Diggle," and a voice, "Going to oppose it.") (Renewed disorder.) The MAYOR having appealed for a bearing, Dr. Manses rem irked that they obtained the preser4a of the chairman of the committee, who ought in the ordinary course of things to have been in the House of Convnons that evening, but he would not break his engagement with them. Us thought Mr. Diggle's sense and generous feeling would at once make him sit down. (Hear, hear.) He had one thing more to say Mr. Denneat : Do you think I shall wait for Mr. Adamson or anybody else. i'llproar.) Mr. Adaineon wants to get away by train and I will give way to him, but I de not want to do i: because I am just as good a man so Mr. Adamson. The resolntion was there carried amid the greatest enthu- siaein. Mr. ADAMSON, who waa received with prolonged cheering, said he was deeply moved by the reception they had given him, and he was most thankful for Mr. Diggle's courteousness —(latigieter)—in having gives way to allow him to speak in rime to catch his train. He confessed he was rejoiced to be in Warrington for the first time to meet the good men of the town, and to hear their enthusiastic approbation of the Manchester Ship Canal, that was, he believed, to do good to Warrington more than to any other town. (Hear, hear,. and [applause.) Warrington was to have a dock of 22 acres in area to begin with and ID acres of an approach, equal to it dock double the size of the dock at Gersten, which bad two millions of tons of shipping. (Applause.) He waa sure that when his friend Mr. Monks said that a small canal might suffice he spoke to the best of his judgment. tti be (Mr. Adamson) thought it would be a for better thing to have one upon which ocean-going steamers could go, as in the case of the Suez Canal. It would no doubt serve the interests of Liverpool to have a barge canal, and Mr. Monks would do well if he could furnish two or three donkeys to do the work. (Laughter.) But t'e himself would en- deavour to furnish them with good substantial draught horses to do the work, and leave the donkeys to Liverpool. (Leughter and applause.) Would it answer their purpose that Mr. Monks or any other trader in Warrington should carry his goods to Liverpool to put them on board ship? ("No.") No, they must place them on board at Warring- ton. (Lead applause.) Why should they play second fiddle to either Liverpool or Manchester? The construction of a Ship Canal was a subject that had been before the public for a a very long time. Its merits and demerits had been fully discasswl, and it pissed through a very severe ordeal last year—through the House of Commons—and it had passed through a not less severe one, but a more successful one, this year, in the House of lahhis. They were now, in their manufacturing industry, harassed by all kinds ot difficulties, which placed !manufacturers at a great dis- advantage in comparison with foreign countries, and it was belie.ved that if the canal WAS constructed it would give an advantage to their manufacturers, and would enable them to have their goods carried at a very much cheaper rate than at present, and would consequently Eive them a larger mar- gin of profit, and, as be was informed, enable them suc- ceseluily in mazy respects to compete with the foreigners, notwithstanding the great disadvanges to which they were at present exposed. Therefore, it seemed scarcely reasonable to believe that those gentlemen who had incurred such great responsibilities, who bad expeaded so much time and trouble, would have incurred all those responsibilities if they had had the least doubt at all about the canal being constructed without any damage being done to the estoary. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD. • xmacirioN OF MEMBERS. On Thursday evening tho annual vestry meeting for the election of three members of the Burial Board was held in Bethesda schoolroom, under the presidency of Mr W Hanley. There were present Messrs James Wright, H Coleburn, U Moss, W Littler, Joseph Shaw, John Sumrnerfield, Thomas , Riley, Thomas Stringfellow, Wild ma Dobson, John Poole, 1 W Sutton (assistant overseer). The retiring members of the Board were Messrs James Handley, JP, Thomas Nor- man, mad George Moss, but they were eligible for re-rlec- tion.-Tho Chairmme in opening the proceedings, observed that the small attendance showed that the public of Runcorn was satisfied with the way in which the business of the town so far as ce3cerne4 tho Burial Board was conducted.—Mr Cole- I burn proposed the appointment of Mr James HandMy as a ' member of the Board. His remarked that he had been an , exc-Ilent member in the past - he took a great interest in • the affaira of the towa, especially in the financial position of a the Burial Board; and he (Mr Coleburn) trusted he would be re-elected.—Mr Stringfellow seconded the motion which was carried unanimously—Mr D Bisbrown proposed the re- elec, ion of Mr Nortnan, who he said, had business qualifi- cations for the position.. He was noted for his geniality, and he was deservedly popular with all Sects and parties. (Hear, hear.) The motion was seconded by Mr Jos W Bayley, and carried unanimously. In proposing the re-election of INtr MOON Mr T Riley said that gentleman had served the town very well on the Board so far, and they would fare worse if they elected any other man,—Mr. James Wright seconded the motion, adding a few complimentary observations.—The motion was passed unanimonely.—The Chairman remarked that the meeting hod passed the best vote of thanks possible to the gentlemen for their past services by again placing them in a position to serve them again.—On the motion of Mr. Stringfellow, seconded by Mr. Colehurn, the overseers were empowered to expend such additional sum, not exceeding £lsi, as required for completing the fitting up of the present Overseers' Office. The Chairman bad previously explained that £2O had been expended in fitting up the new offices in Waterloo House, irst there was some additional furniture wanted to make them eomportable and worthy of the town. Nearly 30 years had elapsed since such an expenditure had been in- curred before.-5 hearty yore of thanks was accorded to Om Chairmen, on the proposal of Mr. Coleburn, seconded by Mr. Moss. both gentlemen speaking in highly eulogistic terms of , Mr. llandley's abilities.

SHOCKING PO.
SONING CASE.

A. shocking death from the effects of poison occurred at Warrington on Wednesday, under the following circum- stances. It appears that a young man named William Neil an, 27 years of age, a labourer, who resided at 29, Dol- man's-lane, had been drinking heavily since the 14th mat, when the militia broke up, and that he had been reduced to such a state of mind that since Sunday he had to be con- stantly watched by his friends. At about I-3(.1 on Wednes- day afternoon he took a bottle containing belladonna (tom 4 table at his home, and before his father, Patrick Nielan, could prevent him, drunk some of the contents. The bottle was labelled "Poison," and the belladonna had been used as a lotion by the mother of the young man. Information of the occurrence was given to the police, and Neihm was con- veyed to the Infirmary in a neighbour's cart, and atLended to by Drs. Richmond and Smith. Despite their exertions, however, he died at about 8-30 in the evening. THE INQUEST.

Yesterday morning, Mr. Briimuse, county coroner, held an inquest relutive to the affair at the White Hurt Inn, Sankey-street, Warrington, when the evidence given below was adduced. Mr. T. Hutton was the foretnan of the Jury.. _ . _

_ Michael Neilan, father of the deceased, said that when the miliria broki up about a fortnight ago, his son began drink- ing heavily, and continued drinking up to shortly before his death. About 1-30 on Wednesday afternoon deceased was sitting near the tire smoking, and the bottle produced Was on the shelf. Witness Saw deceased " grabbing" the bottle, and took it out of his hand. Before witness could. check him he drunk out of the bottle. Witness shouted This is poison," and the deceased said "I'll go to bid now." He went upstairs and threw himself on the bed. tlis mother wont after him, and witness heard him say to her "I can't stand this work, the whole town's running after me." Deceased then ran downstairs and out into the street. and witness ran after him and turned him into the yard. Deceased then vomited, and witness took him into the house, whence he was taken to the Infirmary. After he Was taken into the house he never spoke. The bottle in question had been in the house nearly a year, and contained stuff given to his wife at the Infirmary to rub her leg with.

William Hudson, porter at the Infirmary, said that the deceased was admitted at two o'clock on Wednesday after- noon sufferim,e from poison. Dm. Richmond and Smith cave hint their best attention, but he died shoot 8 30 the same day. Deceased never spoke after being admitted into the Infirmary. The Coroner : It has been given in evidence that Ars. Haan, mother of the person who died, about twelve months ago went to the Dispensary for something to rub her leg with. We believe that bAladonna was given, and that the bottle was simply labelled poison.—Is that the mode at the hospltal ? All that is given out is just labelled wiTh the word" poison."—You did not supply blue fluted bottles to distinguish them from ordinary medicines? We do not supply bottles at all, but use those which people chose to bring.
- The Forernln : Anyone mis,ht get hold of a bottle like that thinking that it was a beer bottle.

The Coroner: It is a beer battle. Addressing the jury, the Coroner said that there was no doubt that the the prisoner was poisoned by the contents of the bottle, and the question was whether it was by misadventure, or whether he knew at the time that the contents were poisonous. It appeared to him a very dangerous practice that people ebonld obtain poison at the Dispensary in bottles, say, that 'had been in household use. If the bottle had previously contained something that the people of the house had b,en in the habit of drinking. it alnaoet followed that they might use it by mistake, and thus unconsciously be the cause of their death. In this case Neilan and his wife were unable to read, ard thouzh the tatter had had the bottle for twelve months she did not know what the label signified, and she only thought it wan poison because it had to be used out- wardly.

The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased committed suicide whilst temporarily insane. The Coroner: Do you wish any presentment as to the manner in which lotions that are poisonous are dispensed at the Hospital ?—The Forem to: I should like to have a report sent there that they should not turn out such bottles.—l suppose you think that sufficient precautions are not taken to guard people from taking the contents? Yes, because a child might he sent with the bottle, and might take some. Inspector Spinks then gave particulars of a similar case that occurred a few weeks ago, in Warrington, when a man Was given poison in mistake for his medicine, and the coro- ner instanced a case that had come under his notice in which a mother had been poisoned by her own daughter in mis- take.

After some further remarks on the subject the Coroner drew up the following presentment t--4' The jurors suggest that better preciutions be taken at the Infirmary when lotions that ate poisons are supp Led to out-patients. The jarers consider that when poison is put ia a beer bottle, the mere 'fact of putting on a label pejoon is not suffi- cient."

div.head: CATERING FOR 'DIE YOUr3G.
div.p: CATERING FOR 'DIE YOUr3G.

Sir,—Tho wonders of the,electric light, electric railways. telephones, dm., convince us that wc are living in an aclYanced'age, and one is led to wonder when the climax will be reached by the introduction of a newly fashioned sckool toy or girl. It really seems to suggest that such a marvelloutt discovery has been made when one thinks of the wsy in which some Sunday scholars were treated during the past week. The people who were responsible for a day's pleasure-to the young seemed to have forgotten that such ' games an " ball," cricket, racing, and a little distribution of toys or sweets had am' Interest for their scholars, and, judg- ing from their disappointment the youngsters seemed to be just as old fashioned as their forefatbem. Surely when Sunday school superintendents take the young folks for an outing they should prorlde them with some little amuse- ment beyond a ride in a crowded carriage and a mug of milk. I venture to take no a little of your much needed space in the hope of prevailing upon those superintendents who have not yet taken their children out to cater a little for their amusement as well as for their stomach, and they will Lind their endeavours are heartily appreciated.—On be- half of their little a11i35, I remain, yours, &e.,

" SUN [MY CLOSING."

Sir,—As an elector with no strong party political bias, but one greatly interested in social questions, I would suggest that it is desirable that the Conservative arid Liberal can- didates s honk% at the earliest possible moment publicly anonnce the position which they take on the all important question of the Sunday closing of public-houses. I can quite understand that Sir G. Greenall may be somewhat dif- filent in expressing his views upon this most important question, but I feel sure that he will not allow his pecuni- ary interests tit outweigh his zoal for the welfare of all classes and his respect for that due observance of the Lord's Day, which, under present circumstances, is to many worthy people an utter impossibility. I may say that my action at the next parliamentary election will be greatly in- fluenced by the position which the two candidates take upon this question, and as it is essential that the electors should know early for whom to vote, I would sug- gest that the Loctl Temperance Society, together with the Church of England Temperance Society, should jointly send a deputation to Sir Gilbert Greenall, and also to Mr. Wm. Ciosfield, for the purpose of ascertaining their repective opinions, with a view to a subsequent public ttion of them —Yours, SOCIAL REFORNIER.

div.head: TORY'S VIEW OF "LIBERALISM."
div.p: A TORY'S VIEW OF "LIBERALISM."

Sir,—" Fair hay" is rather a carious customer. Hav- ing been proved in error as to the writer of a certain letter be quietly drops that point and rushes into others that seem equally beyond his power to grasp. In his first paragraph " Fair Play" exhibits a pitiful amount of bungling, Mixing up trade questions with politics. lie compares the legiti- mate trades carried on by the Ryland's, Broadbent's, Cros• fields' and Monks' with the traffic of Sir Gilbert. If " Fair Play" is capable of thinking out a question, I ask him to give ten minutes to working out the mighty results that would follow suppesing we had the power of saying which of the two—the traffic or the trades—should cease for twelve months. lam no teetotaller, but I think if Sir Gilbert and his beer stayed at the other side of the bridge twelve months we should see a mighty difference. Mind, I don't wish this to come about, eocause some one else might send a worse class of beer into the town, and this would be bad for us pothouse men. Now, as to principles and persons. I suppose it is a fact that we seldom heve principles without persons, and when you attack a man it is on account of his principles. I quite willingly accept it as a fact that Sir Gilbert's principles, in the ordinary sense, are all that is required. But his politics, my friend, what about them? 7, speaking as a working- man, am anxious that he should have no seat in thA next Parliament, beceuse ihs would support a party whose Pot as we have proved in the past, is always ruinous. " Feir Play" wishee me to "enplain what this thing is they cell Liberelism." This question would be soon answered by pointing to a history of England and saying "all that is in this book of a progressive and beneficial character is Liberalism." We are now within a measurable distance of seeing a new Reform Gill pawed. Sneering won't stop it. The coming leader ef the Tory Democratic party has re o- flounced in favour of it, and possibly Lord Salisbury will consider twice before hedeads his party into a position that means neither more nor less than defiance of the people. There are other measures before the country, as fur instance the London Government Bill, and we in the provinces have: something to do with this irnpertant measure. I may refer "Fair Play" to a letter in the Pall Gazette. written by Mr. James Beal. in which the writer gives a sketch of the means taken by Toryism in their opposition to this bill ; of men hired to attend' vtrions meetings who didn't even understand the objact of the meeting; who were , simply paid to brawl, and whose tickete of adrnittance were °rave, and all because the Government wish to make London municipal government in harmeny with nineteenth century ideas. As an instance, and drawing attention to the necessity for reforming the House or Lords, a bill was brought lo—the Hyde Park Corner (Streets) Bill, and it was thrown out. The result is that the maintenance of the new roads which were made in the recent improvements re- mains a charge upon the general taxpayers of the country Instead of being transferred to the ratepayers of the metro- polis. I ask "Fair Play" what reason we have to be thank- ful for the existence of the House of Lords after such work as this " Liberalism"' would alter this. When will Toryism make the attempt? The Rev. a J. Littleton, vicar of Penkridge, srleaking o - the Dissenters, says —"The Dis• enters only kept together because they wanted to plunder a good rich church, and then they would quarrel over the bodes. It was a lie of the Redicals to say the working-man- had to sopport the clergy. When a Radical or Republican like Joseph Arch said the working-men were supporting the clergy, he was a liar." What does " Fair Play" think of this Language from an educated gentleman ? " Liberalism " will most certainly, at an early date, remove from this foul-menthed parson's path the stumbling block of an Established Church. Sir, from the cuttings I have at hand i could supply Fair Play" with such a selection of speeches delivered by parsons of the Established Church as would make him blush for very shame. For pity's sake I withhold my hand, knowing that it will all came about in good time in spttebf Tory screaming. Poiating to Ireland, your correspondent sees nothing BO "plunder and coercion." Will he kindly state how many Tories voted against ceercion,and how many Radical foe it ? For plunder! prefer to take official reports, and there Plied Irish landlords ere in a far more...equitable position than ever they were before. I see a report in the papers that the Eccleshall estate, near Stafford, valued a few yehrs SiDCS at £22000, has just been sold for Mt 000. This in deprecia- tion with a vengeance. Who would "Fair Flay" blame for It? I should blame the inherently rotten system we desig- nate the Lind Leave. Liberals in a few short years will alter this But in the meantime a Land League must be formed capable of proving to our country cousins the great neces- sity there is for land reform ; that as individuals did not make the land, so individuate should nnt own it, in the same sense ase.wning a horse or cow. The nation's welfare must stand before the individual's. The Egyptian question is one that the country tenet insist anon being left in the hands of Mr. Gladstone. Ti) drive him from Miles just now would mean introlceing Jingoism of the meet rabid kind. Annexation and ail its responsi- bilities would crowd upnn us, and this, too, before we have recovered from the ruinous effats of Lord Reaconsfinles LGovernment.—Yorws, , ft WRITHAM.

NORTECOTE formally made the motion that the entry on the journals. be corrected by omission of the words nemine contradieente —Eventually the House divided Hrmsq.divided on Sir S. Nerthcote's. motion—Ayes, 52; noes, 25. Inman SuNDAY CLOSING Brtm.—The adjourned debate on the motion In read the Sale of' Intoxicating Liqnors en Sun- day (Ireland) Rill a second Mite was resumed.—Mr. Wan- TON continued the speech against 'the bill in which be was Prematurely cut short last Tuesday.—Mr. Munn:objected to the bill. He did not see why the nem man should be debarred all refreshment on Sunday, while the rich man had his luxurious club ocien to him on that day.—Mr. T. Dtcx- eon warmly supported the second reading, and urged the Government to press the measure forward, soppooted, as it was, by four-fifths of the Irish people.—Mr. LIMO op- posed the second reading, and ;misted the restrictions that already existed as to Sunday drinking in Ireland were sufd- 'cleat for all parposes —Dr. ',sons having spoken for over an hour, ware proceeding to illustrate the evil effect of , attempting to, interfere arbitrarily with the rights of a great portion of the Irish people, when Mr. CAINE interrupted the bon member and asked the Speaker's opinion whether Dr. Lyons was not within the new rule passed to prevent 1 wilful repetition ?—The SPEAKER, however, decided that I the bon. member was in order, and he proceeded and con- tinned his observations until he talked the biWoott at ten minutes to seven, and the debate was adjourned, • The Criminal Lunatics Bill was referred to the Grand Chmmittee on Law, and the sitting was suspended. •• Paz IfiGHLAND CnorrEtts —The House resumed at 'nine o'clock.—Mr. MaararaLstan called attention to the re- port- of the Royal Commission on the condition of the crofters mid cotters of the Highlands of Scotland. He moved that the report et the commission on the condition of these people demands the immediate attention of the Government with a view to citing legislative and adminis- trative effect- to its recommendations.— Dr. CAMERON seconded the motion, and insisted that the crofters et Scot-

land bad the same right to be protected against eviction as the Irish small farmer.—Mr. A. Berarotra denied that land- lords of Sod ,nct had formed deer forests simply to gratify their Men amusement. —Lord C. Catrerenxt criticised the report and took exception to the statements of the moven—Sir Vf4 HARCOURT admitted the pressing import- ance of the subject. but said, it was surrounded with diffi- culty. All would admit, he said, there was not time to bring in a Scotch land bit) dating the present session.—Mr. atscrestaant ultimately asked leave to withdraw the mo- tion.
The House was counted and forty members wort not present. _ _ _
